title: Gender Sensitisation at Work
tagline: See bias, know the rules, step in with confidence and build a workplace where everyone can thrive: practical gender sensitisation for teams anywhere.
description:
Most gender problems at work are not caused by bad people. They come from habits nobody questions: who gets the late shift, whose idea gets credited, which group-chat 'joke' everyone ignores, and who is quietly left off the promotion list 'for her own good'. This certification helps every employee, manager and HR professional, wherever they work, see those habits clearly and change them.

You will learn the difference between **sex and gender**, how **stereotypes and unconscious bias** shape decisions, and how **equality and equity** work together. You will build a business case a sceptical board will believe, and design policies on **parental leave, flexible work, childcare and safe transport** that people can actually use.

The course starts from the **international standards**: CEDAW, the ILO conventions on equal pay, discrimination and maternity, and **ILO Convention 190** on violence and harassment at work. It then shows how countries such as the US, UK, India, Pakistan, Kenya and Australia turn them into law, and reminds you to check the rules where you work. Real cases from around the world run through every stage. Then you practise: responding to a disclosure, preserving online evidence, stepping in as a bystander, preventing retaliation, welcoming transgender colleagues with dignity, and measuring progress with real numbers.

Five stages, a ten-question test after each, and a tough timed final exam built on realistic international workplace scenarios.
audience: All staff, in any country, who want to understand gender, bias and respectful behaviour at work
Line managers and supervisors who allocate work, appraise people and receive disclosures
HR and people professionals who design policies and support harassment complaint processes
Members of harassment complaint committees and the managers who act on their findings
Senior leaders and diversity champions who set targets and report progress to boards
outcomes: Distinguish sex from gender and recognise stereotypes and unconscious bias in everyday decisions
Explain equality and equity, the main international standards behind them, and present a carefully framed business case for gender inclusion
Explain ILO Convention 190 and how different countries regulate workplace harassment, including employer duties, complaint routes and the need to check local law
Recognise harassment in person and online, respond well to a disclosure and intervene safely as a bystander
Design inclusive policies and meetings, and support women's progression and transgender colleagues with dignity
Measure progress using representation, promotion-rate, attrition and pay-gap data, and report it honestly

quest.name: Mission Equal Footing
quest.premise: You have just joined Group People & Culture at Saffron Line Foods, a tea and biscuit maker with its head office in Dubai, a plant at Thika in Kenya and sales hubs in Singapore, London and Lahore. The engagement survey is alarming: women are leaving, and the exit interviews don't say 'family reasons'. Your mentor, Dr Leila Haddad, has ninety days to build a plan the board will back. With a sceptical COO, a plant manager who learns to speak up, a star sales manager close to resigning and a young engineer facing harassment in a group chat, climb five stages to the Summit Boardroom.

cast.name: Dr Leila Haddad

sessions.title: Sex, Gender, Stereotypes and the Bias We Don't See
sessions.summary: Start with yourself. Learn the difference between sex and gender, how stereotypes turn into everyday decisions, the main forms of unconscious bias at work, and simple habits that interrupt bias before it shapes a hire, a promotion or a joke.
objectives: Distinguish sex from gender, gender roles and gender norms using workplace examples
Explain how descriptive and prescriptive stereotypes, benevolent sexism and the double bind affect women and men at work

cards.title: Day one: the survey nobody wanted to read
cards.setting: Group People & Culture floor, Saffron Line Foods head office, Dubai. 9:15 am.

lines.text: Your first morning in Group People & Culture. A printed report lands on your desk, with three pages flagged in purple.
Welcome. I'm Leila Haddad. This is our engagement survey. Women's scores dropped in every country we operate in, and seven of our last ten manager-level resignations were women.
Leila, with respect, women leave when the children come, or to follow a partner's job. That's life, not a company problem.
Then the exit interviews should say 'family reasons'. Most of them say 'no growth', 'late meetings' or 'I didn't feel safe on the night shift'.
Fine. The board wants a plan in ninety days. If you can show me it's real, I'll back it.
That's our mission. I call it Mission Equal Footing: equal footing for everyone at Saffron Line, from Thika to Singapore. And you're on it.
Stage one is the Mirror Hall. Before we fix the company, we check the assumptions we all carry, me included. Ready to look in the mirror?

cards.title: Sex and gender are not the same thing

scenes.heading: Sex: the biology
scenes.narration: Sex refers to biological characteristics: chromosomes, hormones and reproductive anatomy. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are sex-linked. So is the need for a lactation room.

scenes.heading: Gender: the script society writes
scenes.narration: Gender is the set of roles, behaviours and expectations that a society attaches to being a woman or a man. Who brews the tea, who drives, who stays late. Those are scripts, not biology.

scenes.heading: Scripts change
scenes.narration: Because gender is social, it varies between cultures, between families and over time. Your grandmother's office life looked nothing like a Singapore or Nairobi sales team today.

scenes.heading: Roles and norms
scenes.narration: Gender roles are the tasks people are expected to do. Gender norms are the unwritten rules that reward people who follow those roles and punish those who do not.

scenes.heading: Why it matters at work
scenes.narration: Most workplace problems come from gender scripts, not biology. 'She won't want to travel' is a script. Spotting the difference is the first skill of this mission.

cards.title: Sex or gender? Side by side
cards.caption: A quick test: if it is about bodies, it is usually sex. If it is about expectations, it is gender.

items.label: Basis
items.left: Biological characteristics
items.right: Social roles, behaviours and expectations

items.label: Variation
items.left: Largely consistent across societies
items.right: Varies across cultures, families and time

items.label: Example
items.left: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.right: Expecting the woman to leave early for the school run

items.label: Workplace need
items.left: Maternity leave, a private lactation room
items.right: Fair task allocation, no assumptions about travel

cards.title: Body or script?
cards.prompt: Sort each statement: is it linked to biological sex, or is it a gender expectation that society created?

items.text: Being able to become pregnant
The junior woman in the meeting is expected to serve the tea
Men are expected to be the main earner in the family
Needing breaks to express breast milk after childbirth
Only men are rostered on night shifts
Women are assumed to be 'naturally' suited to HR roles
Growing facial hair
Boys are told not to cry when they are upset

cards.question: Which statement describes gender rather than sex?
options: Only women can breastfeed a newborn
In one generation, women in a city started working in banks and pharmacies in large numbers
Pregnancy can cause fatigue in the first trimester
Men and women have different typical hormone levels
cards.explanation: A change within one generation in which jobs women do is a change in social roles and norms, so it is gender. The other three are biological characteristics, which is sex.

cards.title: How stereotypes do their work
cards.body:
A **stereotype** is a generalisation about a group applied to an individual. Two kinds matter at work:

- **Descriptive** stereotypes say what women or men *are* like: 'women are emotional', 'men are not caring'. They make us misjudge individuals.
- **Prescriptive** stereotypes say what they *should* be like: women should be modest, men should never ask for flexible hours. People who break them are often penalised.

This creates the **double bind**: a woman who is assertive is seen as competent but 'difficult', while one who is gentle is liked but seen as less of a leader. Men face their own version when they ask for paternity leave or say they are struggling.

Watch for **benevolent sexism** too: protective-sounding choices such as 'we won't send her on the upcountry distributor tour, it's too tiring for her'. It sounds kind, but it quietly removes opportunities.

Stereotypes feel like common sense. That is exactly why they need checking.

cards.back: Favouring people who are like us: same university, same home town, same gender, same five-a-side team. It makes 'culture fit' a trap.
Noticing evidence that fits what we already believe and ignoring what doesn't. One late report 'proves' a mother is less committed.
One strong positive (halo) or negative (horns) trait colours the whole judgement of a person.
Crediting a man's success to skill and a woman's to luck or help, and blaming her failures on ability rather than circumstance.
Some groups have to show the same competence repeatedly before it is accepted, while others are judged on potential.
Assuming mothers are less committed or less mobile, so they are skipped for stretch roles, travel or promotion without being asked.

cards.title: The promotion panel
cards.setting: Board room, Dubai head office. Quarterly talent review. Joseph joins by video from Thika; Mei Ling joins from Singapore for her item, then leaves.

lines.text: Next: Regional Head, Middle East, based here in Dubai. Mei Ling Tan beat her targets three years running.
Strong numbers. But she has a two-year-old in Singapore. She won't want to move.
And honestly, she can be a bit aggressive with the distributors. Daniel is calmer. Steady pair of hands.
Daniel closed one deal by pushing a distributor very hard last year. We called it 'drive'.
That's... a fair point. I hadn't thought of it that way.
Nobody here is a bad person. But two biases just walked into this room. Can you name them before we vote?

cards.title: How bias keeps itself alive
cards.caption: Unconscious bias is a mental shortcut. Left alone, its results seem to prove the stereotype right.

items.label: A quick judgement
items.detail: Under time pressure, the brain reaches for a shortcut instead of the evidence.

items.label: Stereotype activated
items.detail: 'Mothers don't relocate' or 'she's too aggressive' fills the gap.

items.label: Skewed decision
items.detail: She is not asked, not shortlisted or rated lower than a man with the same record.

items.label: Fewer chances
items.detail: Without stretch roles she gains less experience and visibility.

items.label: 'See, we were right'
items.detail: Fewer women at senior levels seems to confirm the original stereotype.

cards.title: Real case: the recruiting algorithm that learned bias (2018)
cards.body:
In 2018 Reuters reported that Amazon had built, and then abandoned, an experimental tool that used machine learning to rate job applicants' CVs.

- The system learned from about ten years of past applications, most of them from men, as is common in technical roles.
- According to the report, it learned to mark down CVs that included the word 'women's', as in 'women's chess club captain', and to favour wording more common on men's CVs.
- Engineers tried to correct it but could not be sure it would not find other ways to discriminate. Amazon said the tool was never used by its recruiters as the sole basis for decisions, and the project was dropped.

**Lesson:** bias is not only in people's heads. A tool trained on yesterday's decisions copies yesterday's patterns. That is why 'check the pattern' applies to software as well as to panels.

cards.title: Your move on the panel
cards.situation: Leila nods at you. The panel is about to move on and shortlist Daniel alone. Mei Ling has the stronger results; the concerns raised are that she 'won't want to move' with a young child and is 'a bit aggressive'. Nobody has asked Mei Ling about relocating. What do you say?

choices.text: Say nothing. You are new, and the managers know their people better than you do.
choices.outcome: Daniel is shortlisted alone. Three months later Mei Ling hears she was never considered and starts taking calls from recruiters. Silence let the maternal wall decide.

choices.text: Propose that both are shortlisted, that Mei Ling is asked directly about relocation like any candidate, and that 'aggressive' is tested against the same behaviour standard used for Daniel.
choices.outcome: The panel agrees. Mei Ling says she would move, with a start date after her daughter's school term ends. Applying one standard to both candidates removed two biases without accusing anyone.

choices.text: Argue that Mei Ling should get the role because the company needs more women in senior posts.
choices.outcome: The point is well meant, but it shifts the debate from merit to quotas and makes Mei Ling look like a token. Graham digs in. The real issue, an unfair process, never gets fixed.

choices.text: Message Mei Ling after the meeting to tell her what Joseph and Graham said about her.
choices.outcome: Mei Ling is hurt and angry, trust between her and her managers breaks down, and the panel's deliberations are no longer confidential. The process stays biased, and now it is personal.

cards.title: Spot the bias in the comment
cards.prompt: Match each comment overheard at Saffron Line to the bias it best shows.

pairs.right: 'Hire Tom, he went to my old university and plays in my Sunday football league. He'll fit right in.'
'Priya hit target because her region had an easy year. Marco hit target because he's a closer.'
'Don't put Aisha on the Jakarta launch. She just came back from maternity leave.'
'Let's spare the ladies the factory audit. It's dusty and the hours are long.'
'Yes, Ngozi ran two plant shutdowns well, but let's see her do one more before we trust her with a third.'

cards.title: Five bias interrupters
cards.caption: You cannot switch bias off, but you can design decisions so it has less room to work.

items.label: Agree criteria first
items.detail: Decide what 'good' looks like before you see any names or CVs.

items.label: Use the same questions
items.detail: Structured interviews and appraisals, scored against the criteria.

items.label: Run the flip test
items.detail: Ask: would I say or decide this if the person were a man (or a woman)?

items.label: Ask, don't assume
items.detail: Ask every candidate about mobility or hours. Never decide for them.

items.label: Check the pattern
items.detail: Review ratings and shortlists by gender to spot gaps a single decision hides.

cards.title: Real case: the screen behind the audition (US orchestras)
cards.body:
For decades, top orchestras in the United States hired almost only men. From the 1970s many began holding **blind auditions**, with musicians playing behind a screen so the panel could hear but not see them.

- In 2000 the economists Claudia Goldin and Cecilia Rouse published a well-known study of these auditions. They found the screen raised the chance that women advanced, and estimated it explained part of the rise in women's share of orchestra players, from under 5% around 1970 to about a quarter by the mid-1990s.
- Later reviewers have questioned how large and certain the effect is. The direction of the lesson is widely accepted.
- Goldin went on to win the 2023 Nobel prize in economics for her research on women's work and pay.

**Lesson:** you cannot simply switch bias off, but you can design a process that keeps irrelevant information away from the decision.

cards.question: A manager writes in an appraisal: 'Ayesha is too emotional in client meetings.' Using the flip test, what is the best first step?
options: Remove the comment, because appraisals should never mention behaviour
Ask what specific behaviour happened, and whether the same behaviour from a male colleague would be described the same way
Accept the comment, because the manager saw the meetings and HR did not
Ask Ayesha to attend a training course on managing emotions
cards.explanation: The flip test asks whether the same behaviour from someone of another gender would be judged the same way, and it starts with concrete behaviour. Behaviour can be appraised; vague labels such as 'emotional' often carry stereotypes. Sending her to training accepts the label without checking it.

cards.title: Inclusive language, without the lecture
cards.body:
You do not need a new vocabulary, just a little care:

- Use roles, not gender: **chairperson**, **staff hours**, **salesperson**, **team**.
- Drop put-downs that use gender as an insult, such as telling a man to 'man up' or saying someone runs 'like a girl'.
- Skip questions about marriage, children or 'good news' unless the person raises them.
- Comment on work, not looks or clothes.
- Address people as they prefer: first name, title, 'Sir' or 'Madam' are all fine when used for everyone equally.

If you slip, say 'sorry, let me rephrase' and move on. No drama needed.

cards.title: Zara's first month on the shop floor
cards.body:
Zara Hussain, a process engineer on the group graduate programme, is the first woman engineer on the production lines at the Thika plant.

- In week one, the shift supervisor sends every maintenance query to her male junior, assuming he is the engineer.
- Joseph, meaning well, keeps her off the night shift 'for her safety', so she misses the line trials that count for confirmation.
- In meetings, her idea to cut oven downtime is ignored, then praised when a male colleague repeats it.

None of this was malicious. Each choice followed a gender script. Together they told Zara she did not belong.

The fix was simple once named: Joseph asked Zara what she needed for night shifts (safe transport and a working women's washroom), introduced her clearly as the engineer, and started crediting ideas by name in the meeting minutes.

cards.question: Joseph kept Zara off night shifts 'for her safety' without asking her, and she missed line trials that count for confirmation. Which concept best describes this?
options: Affinity bias
Hostile sexism
Benevolent sexism
Confirmation bias
cards.explanation: A protective-sounding decision that removes an opportunity is benevolent sexism. It is not hostile in tone, which is why it is easy to miss. The right approach is to ask her and solve the real safety issue, such as transport.

cards.title: Mirror Hall cleared
items: Sex is biological; gender is the social script of roles, behaviours and expectations, and it changes across cultures and time.
Descriptive stereotypes misjudge individuals; prescriptive ones punish people who break the script, creating the double bind.
Benevolent sexism sounds protective but removes opportunities; ask, don't assume.
Affinity, confirmation, attribution, halo/horns, prove-it-again and the maternal wall all shape hiring and promotion.
Interrupt bias with agreed criteria, structured questions, the flip test and a look at the pattern across decisions.
Process design works: blind auditions helped more women advance in orchestras, while a CV-scoring tool trained on past hiring learned to mark women down.
Inclusive language is about roles not gender, work not looks, and no gender-based insults.

cards.prompt: Think of a recent decision you made about a colleague: an assignment, a rating, a late-night task. Run the flip test on it. Would you have decided the same way if the person were of another gender? What would you check next time?

quiz.question: Which of these is the best description of 'gender' as used in workplace training?
options: The biological characteristics, such as chromosomes and hormones, that distinguish women and men
The roles, behaviours and expectations a society attaches to being a woman or a man
The sex recorded on a person's national identity card at the time it was issued
A legal category that decides which labour laws apply to an employee
quiz.explanation: Gender is social: the roles, behaviours and expectations attached to being a woman or a man, and it varies across cultures and time. Biological characteristics describe sex, not gender.

quiz.question: A plant installs a private lactation room and also stops automatically assigning meeting minutes to the youngest woman present. Which statement is correct?
options: The lactation room responds to a sex-linked need; the minutes change addresses a gender expectation
Both changes respond to biological sex differences
Both changes address gender expectations only
The lactation room addresses a gender expectation; the minutes change responds to a sex-linked need
quiz.explanation: Breastfeeding is biological, so the lactation room responds to a sex-linked need. Who takes the minutes is a social expectation, so changing that addresses gender.

quiz.question: 'Women should be modest and not push for a raise.' What kind of stereotype is this?
options: A descriptive stereotype, because it describes how women typically behave
Affinity bias, because it favours people similar to the speaker
A prescriptive stereotype, because it says how women ought to behave
A sex-linked fact, because it reflects a biological difference
quiz.explanation: Prescriptive stereotypes say how a group should behave and penalise people who break the script. Descriptive stereotypes claim to describe how a group is.

quiz.question: A female manager who gives direct feedback is called 'harsh', while her male peer doing the same is called 'decisive'. If she softens her style, she is called 'not leadership material'. What is this pattern called?
options: The halo effect
Confirmation bias
The maternal wall
The double bind
quiz.explanation: The double bind means a woman is penalised either way: assertive and seen as unlikeable, or warm and seen as less competent. The halo effect is one trait colouring the whole judgement.

quiz.question: A sales director decides not to send the only woman on his team to a three-day distributor conference in another region because 'the travel would be too tiring for her'. She was not asked. What is the best description?
options: Reasonable care, because a manager is responsible for staff welfare on travel
Benevolent sexism that removes an opportunity without asking her
Hostile sexism, because the manager dislikes women in sales
Affinity bias, because he prefers to travel with men
quiz.explanation: The decision sounds protective but takes away a development opportunity on the basis of gender, without her input. That is benevolent sexism. Real welfare care means asking her and addressing any genuine travel or safety needs.

quiz.question: A hiring manager says, 'Let's take Hassan; he went to my university and plays in the same weekend football league, so he'll fit in.' Which bias is most clearly at work?
options: Attribution bias
Prove-it-again bias
Affinity bias
Benevolent sexism
quiz.explanation: Affinity bias is favouring people similar to ourselves. 'Fit' based on shared background is a common way it enters hiring.

quiz.question: Two officers both exceed target. The appraisal says the man 'drove results through strong negotiation', while the woman 'benefited from a favourable territory'. Which bias does this most clearly show?
options: Attribution bias
Affinity bias
Halo effect
Maternal wall
quiz.explanation: Attribution bias credits one group's success to skill and another's to luck or circumstances. The same result has been explained differently by gender.

quiz.question: What does the 'flip test' ask a decision-maker to do?
options: Reverse the order in which candidates are interviewed to avoid fatigue
Ask a colleague of the other gender to review the decision and make the final call in your place
Give the candidate a chance to reply to any negative comment
Check whether the same decision or comment would be made if the person were of another gender
quiz.explanation: The flip test swaps the gender in your mind and asks whether you would still say or decide the same thing. It is a quick way to surface a stereotype.

quiz.question: Which change to a promotion process most directly reduces the chance that bias shapes the result?
options: Letting each panel member use their own judgement of 'leadership presence'
Agreeing the criteria before reviewing candidates and scoring everyone against them
Asking line managers to nominate the people they feel most comfortable with
Deciding in a quick meeting so people rely on their first impressions
quiz.explanation: Criteria agreed in advance and applied to everyone leave less room for shortcuts and stereotypes. Vague 'presence', comfort and first impressions are exactly where bias operates.

quiz.question: In a team meeting a manager says to a male officer who missed a target, 'Come on, stop acting like a girl. Man up if you can't handle it.' What is the best view?
options: It's harmless banter that men in sales teams are used to, and it was aimed at a man, not at women
It is only a problem if a woman is present in the meeting
It is inappropriate, because it uses gender as an insult and demeans women and the officer
It is fine if the officer laughs along at the time
quiz.explanation: Using femininity as an insult demeans women and shames the man for not fitting a gender script. Whether women are present or the target laughs does not make it acceptable.

sessions.title: Equality, Equity and the Case for Change
sessions.summary: Build a case the board will believe. Separate equality from equity, use well-established evidence without overclaiming, anchor the case in international standards such as CEDAW and the ILO conventions, and design practical policies on leave, flexible work, childcare and safe transport that actually get used.
objectives: Explain the difference between equality and equity and why equity measures are not favours
Present a business case for gender inclusion using carefully framed evidence
Identify the main international standards on equal pay, non-discrimination, maternity protection and family responsibilities, and how countries build on them
Design inclusive policies on parental leave, flexible work, day-care and safe transport
Distinguish a policy that exists on paper from one that people can use without penalty

cards.title: Show me the numbers
cards.setting: COO's office, group head office, Dubai. Late afternoon, coffee going cold.

lines.text: I read your Mirror Hall notes. Fair points. But I run a profit and loss account, not a debating society. Why should Saffron Line spend money on this?
Because we are paying already. Every manager who resigns costs us recruitment, training and lost sales. We just don't see it on one line.
(on speaker from Singapore) And I'm not asking for less work, Graham. I'm asking for a different shape of work. Two days from home would keep me.
At the plant, Zara's problem is simpler. The last staff bus leaves at 7 pm on an unlit road. The night line trials end at 10.
So we treat everyone the same and let them sort out their own transport. That's equality, isn't it?
Same treatment for people starting from different places doesn't give the same chance. Welcome to the Ledger Room. Let's balance the books properly.

scenes.heading: Equality: the same for everyone
scenes.narration: Equality means treating everyone the same: the same rules, the same bus, the same leave. It is a good starting point and it is the goal for rights and pay for equal work.

scenes.heading: When 'the same' isn't fair
scenes.narration: But people start from different places. One staff bus at 7 pm treats everyone equally, yet only the engineer who cannot safely walk an unlit road at 10 pm loses the chance to attend trials.

scenes.heading: Equity: fair treatment for different needs
scenes.narration: Equity means adjusting support so that everyone has a genuinely fair chance. A late-shift drop service for anyone on night trials is an equity measure.

scenes.heading: Equity serves equality
scenes.narration: Equity is the route, equality of opportunity is the destination. Equity measures are not favours or lower standards. Everyone still meets the same bar.

scenes.heading: International law agrees
scenes.narration: The UN women's rights convention, known as CEDAW, bans discrimination against women. It also says that temporary special measures to speed up real equality are not discrimination. Equality and equity sit side by side.

cards.title: Equality or equity in practice
cards.caption: Both have a place. Equity closes the gap so that equal rules become fair in reality.

items.label: Transport
items.left: One staff bus at 7 pm for all
items.right: Drop service for anyone on late shifts

items.label: Promotion
items.left: Same criteria for all candidates
items.right: Same criteria, plus sponsorship for groups who lack networks

items.label: Facilities
items.left: One shared washroom block
items.right: Separate, safe, lockable facilities for women

items.label: Standard
items.left: Same bar for everyone
items.right: Same bar for everyone: support changes, standards don't

cards.question: A pharma company offers a late-evening drop service to every employee whose field visits end after 8 pm, after women reps said they were turning down evening doctor meetings. Which statement is most accurate?
options: It is a favour for women that lowers standards for men
It breaks the principle of equality, because some staff get a service others don't
It is an equity measure that removes a barrier so everyone can meet the same targets
It is only needed if the law specifically requires it
cards.explanation: Equity adjusts support to remove barriers so everyone has a fair chance to meet the same standard. The targets are unchanged and the service is available to anyone working late, so no standard is lowered.

cards.title: The global picture in four numbers
cards.caption: Real figures, rounded. Say where they come from, present studies as links rather than proof, and check the latest edition before you present them.

items.label: Women in the labour force
items.detail: ILO estimates put women's global labour force participation just under half, against over 70% for men.

items.label: Years to close the gap
items.detail: Recent World Economic Forum Global Gender Gap Reports estimate well over a century at the current pace.

items.label: Diverse executive teams
items.detail: McKinsey (2020): top-quartile firms for gender diversity were more likely to have above-average profits. A link, not proof of cause.

items.label: Share of customers
items.detail: Women are about half the population, so about half of potential customers, patients and account holders.

cards.title: A business case that survives the boardroom
cards.body:
Five strands a sceptical board will accept:

- **Talent**: hiring from only half the population shrinks the pool. Graduates are increasingly women in many fields.
- **Retention cost**: replacing a manager means recruitment fees, months of ramp-up and lost relationships. Calculate it from your own data.
- **Customers**: women influence household spending, health choices and savings. Teams that reflect customers design better products.
- **Decisions**: varied teams challenge groupthink and spot risks earlier.
- **Risk and law**: harassment and discrimination bring legal, regulatory and reputational damage.

Frame evidence honestly. Studies showing that diverse firms do better show a **correlation**, not proof that diversity alone *causes* profit. Say so; boards trust presenters who don't overclaim.

And keep the **rights case** beside the business case: fair treatment is required by law and values even when it does not pay off in a quarter.

cards.title: Solid claim or overclaim?
cards.prompt: Leila is checking slides for the board. Sort each statement: is it a solid, defensible claim, or an overclaim she should rewrite?

items.text: Gender diversity guarantees higher profits
Global studies link gender-diverse leadership teams with above-average profitability
Our exit data show 7 of the last 10 manager resignations were women
Hiring one woman manager will raise our sales by 20%
Replacing a manager costs us recruitment fees and months of lost productivity, based on last year's cases
Every company that ignores gender will fail within five years
ILO estimates show women's labour force participation worldwide is well below men's

cards.title: Where equality rules come from
cards.caption: Higher layers set the frame; the lower layers decide what people actually experience on a Tuesday afternoon.

items.label: International standards
items.detail: UN and ILO conventions such as CEDAW, equal pay, non-discrimination and maternity protection.

items.label: National laws
items.detail: Constitutions plus equality, labour, leave and harassment laws. They differ by country, and sometimes by state or province.

items.label: Regulators and sector rules
items.detail: For example, stock-exchange rules on board diversity or a banking regulator's gender policy.

items.label: Company policy
items.detail: Code of conduct, leave, flexible work, transport and grievance procedures.

items.label: Daily practice
items.detail: What managers actually approve, say and tolerate.

cards.title: International standards on your side
cards.prompt: Match each international standard to what it broadly says. (Paraphrased; countries that ratify a convention turn it into their own law.)

pairs.right: Equal pay for women and men for work of equal value
No discrimination, including on the basis of sex, in access to jobs, training and conditions of work
Maternity protection, including at least 14 weeks of maternity leave and protection from dismissal
Workers with family responsibilities, women and men, should be able to work without discrimination
UN convention on women's rights: temporary special measures to speed up real equality are not discrimination

cards.title: Policies on paper
cards.setting: Video call: Dubai, Singapore and the Thika plant. Leila shares the group HR policy manual on screen.

lines.text: Good news: we already have a flexible work policy. Bad news: in three years, only two people have used it.
Because the last person who asked was told she 'wasn't serious about her career'. Everyone heard about it.
Same at the plant. We have paternity leave, three days. No man has taken it. They'd be teased for a month.
And the policy says 'transport on request'. But I have to ask my shift supervisor every single time, and he sighs.
So a policy isn't real until people can use it without paying a price. Let's design them properly.

cards.back: Paid leave around childbirth. The ILO standard is at least 14 weeks; many countries go further. Good practice adds job protection, a phased return and no appraisal penalty.
Paid leave for fathers or second parents. Rules vary widely by country; check yours. When men actually take it, care stops being seen as 'women's work'.
Options such as remote days, staggered hours or compressed weeks, open to all roles where the work allows, judged on output.
On-site crèche, partner centre or allowance. Some laws require it: India, since 2017, for establishments with 50 or more employees.
A private, clean, lockable room (not a washroom) with a fridge and break time for mothers returning from leave.
Pick-and-drop for late or early shifts, verified drivers, safe routes and a rule about who is dropped last.
A planned re-entry after leave or a career break: keep-in-touch days, a buddy, refresher training and a clear role.

cards.title: Mei Ling's request
cards.situation: Mei Ling formally requests to work from home on Mondays and Fridays for six months while her daughter settles into school. Her role is mostly calls, reports and distributor reviews; she visits the market Tuesday to Thursday. Her line manager, Arjun, forwards the request to you with the note: 'If I say yes, everyone will want it.' How do you advise him?

choices.text: Decline it; making exceptions creates unfairness and Mei Ling can resign if it doesn't suit her.
choices.outcome: Mei Ling resigns two months later and joins a competitor with her distributor relationships. Replacing her takes five months. 'No exceptions' cost far more than the flexibility would have.

choices.text: Approve it quietly as a personal favour, and ask Mei Ling not to tell anyone.
choices.outcome: Mei Ling stays, but colleagues notice and resent the 'secret deal'. The next request is refused by a different manager. A hidden favour creates exactly the unfairness Arjun feared.

choices.text: Assess it against the role's needs and the policy, agree output measures and a review date, and apply the same approach to any future request from anyone.
choices.outcome: Arjun approves a six-month trial with clear targets. Mei Ling's numbers hold. Two other staff, including a man caring for his father, apply under the same rules. Fair, visible and manageable.

cards.title: Designing a safe transport policy
cards.prompt: Joseph wants a late-shift transport policy for the plant that people will actually trust. Put the steps in the best order.
steps: Map the risk: shift end times, routes, lighting and where staff live
Consult the people affected, including women on late shifts, in a safe setting
Design the service: pick-and-drop, verified drivers, safe drop order and an emergency contact
Write it into policy so it applies automatically, with no per-trip permission needed
Communicate it to all staff and supervisors
Monitor use, incidents and feedback, then adjust

cards.title: Leave and care: the global floor and local rules
cards.body:
Leave rules differ a great deal between countries, so always **check the law where each of your people works**.

- **The international floor:** ILO Convention 183 sets at least **14 weeks** of maternity leave, with cash benefits and protection from dismissal.
- **Country examples:** the UK allows up to 52 weeks of statutory maternity leave, not all of it paid. US federal law gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave. Sweden gives parents 480 days of paid parental leave per child, with 90 reserved for each parent.
- **Fathers:** paternity leave is newer in many places. Pakistan's recent federal law for Islamabad, for example, introduced paid paternity leave.

Good employers treat the law as the floor. They make leave **gender-neutral where possible** (so mothers don't become the 'expensive' hire), protect appraisals during leave and plan the return.

cards.question: Saffron Line already offers three days' paternity leave, but no man has taken it in three years. What is the most likely issue and fix?
options: Men don't need leave, so the policy should be withdrawn
The leave is too long and should be cut to one day
The problem is legal, so the company should wait for a new law
A gender norm makes using it costly; senior men taking it visibly and managers endorsing it would help
cards.explanation: A policy that exists but is never used usually has a cultural cost attached. Visible role models and managers who endorse it remove the stigma. Withdrawing or shortening it would reinforce the idea that care is women's work.

cards.title: The Singapore flexible-work pilot
cards.body:
After Mei Ling's trial, Leila ran a six-month pilot across the Singapore sales office.

- **Rules**: any role could apply; managers judged requests on the job's needs, agreed output targets and set a review date.
- **Uptake**: 14 of 38 staff applied, 6 of them men. Requests included school runs, an MBA and caring for a parent.
- **Results**: sales targets were met, and voluntary resignations fell compared with the same period last year. Leila reported this as encouraging, not as proof, since the market also improved.
- **Lesson**: open to everyone, visible rules and output measures made flexibility normal rather than a 'mothers' favour'.

Graham read the one-page summary twice. 'Fine,' he said. 'Now do the plant.'

cards.title: Real case: Sweden's 'daddy months'
cards.body:
In 1974 Sweden became the first country to replace maternity leave with **parental leave** that either parent could take. On paper it was equal. In practice, fathers took almost none of it.

- In **1995** Sweden reserved one month of paid leave for each parent: use it or lose it.
- A second reserved month followed in **2002** and a third in **2016**. Today 90 of the 480 days per child are reserved for each parent.
- Fathers' share of parental-leave days rose from almost nothing in the 1970s to around 30% in recent years.

**Lesson:** a gender-neutral policy is not enough if a norm makes one group pay a price for using it. Reserving well-paid leave for fathers made taking it normal, which also made mothers less of an 'expensive' hire.

cards.title: Ledger Room balanced
items: Equality is the same treatment; equity adjusts support to remove barriers so everyone can meet the same standard.
A credible business case uses talent, retention cost, customers, decision quality and risk, and presents studies as correlations, not guarantees.
International standards set the floor: ILO conventions on equal pay (C100), non-discrimination (C111), maternity (C183, 14+ weeks) and family duties (C156); CEDAW allows temporary special measures.
Inclusive policies cover parental leave, flexible work, day-care, lactation rooms, safe transport and return-to-work support.
A policy is real only when people can use it without a career penalty; gender-neutral design helps.
Reserved, well-paid leave for fathers changes norms: Sweden's 'daddy months' raised fathers' share of leave from almost nothing to around 30%.
Leave and care laws differ by country (and sometimes by state or province) and change often: always check the current version where your people work.

cards.prompt: Pick one policy in your organisation that exists on paper. Who actually uses it, and who doesn't? What unwritten cost might be stopping people, and what one change would make it genuinely usable?

quiz.question: Which statement best describes equity in a workplace setting?
options: Giving every employee exactly the same resources and rules, regardless of their individual circumstances
Setting lower performance standards for groups that have faced barriers
Adjusting support so people facing different barriers have a fair chance to meet the same standard
Hiring equal numbers of women and men in every department
quiz.explanation: Equity adjusts support, not standards, so that everyone has a genuinely fair chance. Identical resources is equality; lowering standards or rigid number-matching is neither.

quiz.question: A bank's only staff van leaves the regional office at 6 pm. Women officers decline month-end late duties that are counted in promotion decisions. Which response is an equity measure?
options: Remove month-end duties from the promotion criteria for women only
Keep the van at 6 pm because it is the same for everyone
Ask women officers to arrange their own transport if they want promotion
Provide a late drop for anyone working month-end duties
quiz.explanation: A late drop for anyone on late duties removes the barrier while keeping the same promotion criteria for all. Changing the criteria for women only lowers the standard rather than removing the barrier.

quiz.question: A consultant tells your board: 'Studies prove that adding women to the executive team will increase your profits.' What is the most accurate correction?
options: Studies link gender-diverse leadership with above-average profitability, but a link is not proof of cause
Studies show diversity has no relationship with company performance
The claim is correct, is backed by every major global study, and should be presented to the board as a guarantee
No research exists on this topic, so it should not be mentioned
quiz.explanation: The research shows a correlation. Presenting it as proof of cause overclaims and undermines trust. Saying no research exists or no link exists is also wrong.

quiz.question: Which international standard states that temporary special measures to speed up real equality between women and men are not discrimination?
options: ILO Convention 100 on equal remuneration
CEDAW, the UN convention on women's rights
ILO Convention 183 on maternity protection
ILO Convention 156 on family responsibilities
quiz.explanation: CEDAW, the UN women's rights convention, says temporary special measures aimed at speeding up real equality are not discrimination. ILO Convention 100 is about equal pay for work of equal value, not special measures.

quiz.question: Which ILO convention sets an international minimum of 14 weeks of maternity leave?
options: Convention 100
Convention 111
Convention 156
Convention 183
quiz.explanation: ILO Convention 183 (2000) on maternity protection sets at least 14 weeks of maternity leave with cash benefits and protection from dismissal. Convention 156 concerns workers with family responsibilities.

quiz.question: A company has a flexible work policy, but it has been used twice in three years and staff say requesters are seen as 'not serious'. What does this best show?
options: A policy is not real until people can use it without a career penalty
Staff do not want flexibility, so the policy can be withdrawn
The policy should be restricted to women so it is used more
Flexible work only suits head-office roles
quiz.explanation: Low use plus reported stigma means the policy has a hidden cost. Restricting it to women would deepen the stigma; the fix is visible, fair rules and manager support.

quiz.question: Why do many employers make parental leave and flexible work policies gender-neutral?
options: Because the law always requires identical leave for mothers and fathers
Because women do not need maternity-specific provisions
So care is shared and women are not seen as the only 'costly' hires
So the company can reduce maternity leave to match paternity leave
quiz.explanation: Gender-neutral design shares care between parents and reduces the perception that hiring women is more costly. Maternity-specific needs such as recovery and breastfeeding still remain.

quiz.question: An HR officer is opening a new sales office in Nairobi for a group headquartered in Dubai. She wants to confirm how many weeks of paid maternity leave the company must provide there. What is the best approach?
options: Use the figure from a group training slide from several years ago
Check the current law of the country where the office is, using the ILO's 14 weeks only as a reference floor
Apply the head-office country's rule, since a group-wide policy set in Dubai overrides local law in every country
Copy the policy of a competitor that operates in a different country
quiz.explanation: Leave laws differ by country and change often, and local law applies to people working there. The ILO minimum of 14 weeks is a useful reference, but she must check the current national (and any local) rules. A group policy can be more generous, not less.

quiz.question: Which room setup meets good practice for mothers returning from maternity leave?
options: A private, clean, lockable room that is not a washroom, with a fridge and agreed break time
A spare cubicle in the women's washroom
The multi-faith quiet room, between other bookings
A corner of the canteen with a screen
quiz.explanation: A lactation room should be private, hygienic, lockable and not a washroom, with refrigeration and protected break time. Shared or public spaces fail on privacy and hygiene.

quiz.question: When designing a late-shift transport policy, which step should come before designing the service itself?
options: Communicating the new policy to all supervisors
Monitoring incidents and feedback
Writing the service into the HR manual
Consulting the people affected, including women on late shifts
quiz.explanation: Map the risk and consult those affected first, then design, write into policy, communicate and monitor. Designing without consultation often misses the real problem.

sessions.title: Harassment Law: Global Standards, Local Rules
sessions.summary: Know the rules before you need them. Learn the global standard set by ILO Convention 190, how countries such as the US, UK, India, Pakistan, Kenya and Australia turn it into law, what employers must do, how a fair inquiry works, which outside routes exist, and why you must always check the rules where you work.
objectives: Explain how ILO Convention 190 describes violence and harassment at work, and the people and places it covers
Compare common legal models (harassment as discrimination, dedicated laws with committees, duties to prevent) using examples from several countries
List an employer's core duties: a policy, risk assessment, training, a trained impartial committee and protection from retaliation
Describe a fair internal inquiry, proportionate outcomes, the treatment of false complaints and external routes
Recognise when criminal and online-abuse laws also apply, and why local rules must always be checked

cards.title: The screenshots
cards.setting: Leila's office, group head office, Dubai. 8:40 pm. A video call from the Thika plant in Kenya.

lines.text: I'm sorry to call so late. I've sent you screenshots. Victor, my shift supervisor, messages me after midnight. 'You looked beautiful today.' 'Why don't you reply?' I've asked him to stop. Twice.
And today someone in the 'Shift B' chat group posted an edited photo of me. Twenty-six people saw it. Some laughed.
Thank you for telling me, Zara. You did the right thing, and you're not in trouble. Please keep every screenshot.
(joining the call) Leila, I'll have a word with Victor. But the group is on personal phones, not at work. Is that even our business?
It's very much our business, Joseph, and 'a word' isn't the process. There's a group policy, Kenyan law and an international standard behind both.
Stage three is the Code Wall. Let's learn exactly what the rules say, so that Zara gets a fair process and so does Victor.

scenes.heading: A first global treaty
scenes.narration: In 2019 the International Labour Organization adopted Convention 190, the first international treaty on violence and harassment in the world of work. It came into force in 2021. Countries that ratify it commit to building it into national law.

scenes.heading: What it covers
scenes.narration: It describes violence and harassment as unacceptable behaviour, or threats of it, once or repeated, that aims at or causes physical, psychological, sexual or economic harm. Gender-based harassment is expressly included.

scenes.heading: Who it protects
scenes.narration: Not only employees. It covers people whatever their contract, including interns, apprentices, volunteers, job seekers and people whose job has ended, in the public, private and informal economy.

scenes.heading: Where it applies
scenes.narration: Wherever work happens: the workplace, work trips, training, events and social activities, work-related messages and calls, employer-provided housing, and the journey to and from work.

scenes.heading: What employers should do
scenes.narration: Adopt a policy after consulting workers, include these risks in health and safety management, assess the hazards, and give people information and training. Each country's law sets the details.

cards.title: Milestones: global and local
cards.caption: Years the rulings and laws were made. Many have been amended since, so always check the current version where you work.

items.label: US: the Meritor ruling
items.detail: Supreme Court: harassment that creates a hostile working environment is sex discrimination.

items.label: India: Vishaka guidelines
items.detail: Supreme Court sets binding rules on workplace sexual harassment until Parliament legislates.

items.label: UK and Pakistan laws
items.detail: UK Equality Act bans harassment at work; Pakistan passes its workplace harassment Act (amended 2022).

items.label: India: workplace Act
items.detail: Internal Committees become a legal duty for workplaces with 10 or more employees.

items.label: ILO Convention 190
items.detail: First global treaty on violence and harassment at work. In force from 2021.

items.label: Australia: positive duty
items.detail: After the 2020 Respect@Work inquiry, employers must take measures to prevent sexual harassment.

items.label: UK: prevention duty
items.detail: Employers must take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of their employees.

cards.back: The person who raises the complaint. Anyone can be a complainant, whatever their gender: harassment of men is covered by C190 and most laws.
The person the complaint is about. They have a right to know the allegations and to answer them before any decision.
The organisation's own trained panel that hears complaints. Some laws fix its make-up: India's is led by a senior woman; Pakistan's has three members, at least one a woman.
The senior official who acts on the committee's findings and applies any sanction. Some laws give this role a formal title.
An independent body outside the organisation: an ombudsperson, equality body, labour tribunal or court, depending on the country.
The written standard of behaviour and how to complain. C190 expects it to be made with workers; many laws require it to be displayed or shared.

cards.title: Three legal models around the world
cards.body:
Countries build the international standard into law in different ways:

- **Harassment as discrimination.** US courts treat sexual harassment as sex discrimination under the Civil Rights Act 1964. The UK Equality Act 2010 and EU equal-treatment law ban harassment related to sex and of a sexual nature. Claims go to equality bodies, tribunals or courts.
- **Dedicated laws with internal committees.** India's 2013 Act requires an Internal Committee, led by a senior woman, in workplaces with 10 or more employees. Pakistan's 2010 Act requires a three-member inquiry committee with at least one woman, plus an ombudsperson; a 2022 amendment added gender discrimination and widened 'employee' and 'workplace'.
- **Duties to prevent.** Australia (2022) and the UK (2024) require employers to act to prevent sexual harassment, not just respond.

Labour codes add more: Kenya's Employment Act 2007 requires a sexual harassment policy where there are 20 or more employees.

cards.title: Harassment or normal conduct?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation at Saffron Line: does it call for action as harassment or gender-based mistreatment, or is it normal workplace conduct?

items.text: A supervisor keeps sending late-night personal messages after being asked to stop
An edited photo of a colleague is posted in a work chat group
A manager gives fair, specific feedback on missed delivery targets
Confirmation is made conditional on agreeing to 'private dinners'
A colleague invites a co-worker to a team lunch once, accepts 'no' and never asks again
A woman engineer is deliberately kept off all site work because 'women don't belong on the floor'
Two colleagues disagree loudly about a budget, with no personal or gendered remarks
Repeated sexual jokes are aimed at a colleague who has shown they are unwelcome

cards.title: The employer's core duties
cards.caption: Drawn from ILO Convention 190 and common national laws. Your local law may add specific requirements.

items.label: Write the policy with workers
items.detail: Set the standard, how to complain, and what happens next. Consult staff or their representatives.

items.label: Assess the risks
items.detail: Late shifts, travel, clients, isolated work and online groups. Treat it as part of health and safety.

items.label: Make it visible
items.detail: Display and share it in the languages staff understand, including for contractors and interns.

items.label: Set up a trained committee
items.detail: Impartial, gender-balanced, conflicts declared. Some laws fix its make-up.

items.label: Train, protect and record
items.detail: Train managers and members, guard confidentiality, prevent retaliation and keep case records.

cards.question: Saffron Line's Thika plant forms a harassment committee of three senior male managers 'because they are the most experienced'. What is the main problem?
options: Nothing, as long as they are senior
Committees must be made up of outside lawyers
It lacks gender balance, which good practice expects and some national laws require
Committees must have exactly five members
cards.explanation: Gender balance helps complainants trust the process, and some laws require it: Pakistan's committee needs at least one woman of three, and India's is led by a senior woman. Seniority helps but cannot replace that. Outside lawyers are not generally required.

cards.title: Real case: Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson (US, 1986)
cards.body:
Mechelle Vinson, a bank employee in Washington DC, said her supervisor had pressured her into sexual relations and harassed her over several years. The bank argued it was not responsible, and that she had not lost pay or promotion.

In 1986 the US Supreme Court ruled unanimously that:

- Sexual harassment that creates a **hostile or abusive working environment** is sex discrimination under the Civil Rights Act 1964, even with no lost pay or promotion.
- The key question is whether the conduct was **unwelcome**, not whether the employee 'voluntarily' went along with it.

The case set out the two classic forms of harassment that laws worldwide now recognise: 'do this or else' pressure, and a hostile environment.

**Lesson:** going along with something out of fear is not consent. Ask whether the conduct was welcome.

cards.title: Inside or outside?
cards.setting: Plant meeting room, Thika. Joseph and Leila, with the group harassment policy pinned to the wall behind them.

lines.text: I've read the policy. So Zara has to complain to our committee? Victor's uncle sits on it.
Then he steps aside from this case. And she has choices: our internal process, or routes outside the company. If any of it is a crime, she can go to the police at any time.
And if she goes inside and doesn't like the outcome? Or if Victor thinks it's unfair?
Both can appeal, and the courts remain open. Some countries also have a special external body, like Pakistan's harassment ombudsperson. That's why our process must be clean from day one.
And if it turns out to be false?
Deliberately false complaints can be dealt with. But a complaint that can't be proved is not a false one. Let's walk through it.

cards.title: Internal and external routes
cards.caption: Which external routes exist depends on the country. Criminal conduct can also be reported to the police at any time.

items.label: Who runs it
items.left: The organisation's own trained committee
items.right: An ombudsperson, equality body, tribunal or court

items.label: When used
items.left: First port of call where trust exists
items.right: Directly where the law allows, or on appeal

items.label: Outcome
items.left: Findings to a decision-maker, who applies workplace sanctions
items.right: Binding decisions, orders or compensation

items.label: Examples
items.left: India's Internal Committee, a company's own harassment panel
items.right: Pakistan's ombudsperson, UK employment tribunals, the US EEOC

cards.title: The inquiry, step by step
cards.prompt: Put the stages of a fair internal inquiry in order. (Laws such as India's set short time limits for several steps; check the rules where you work.)
steps: A written complaint reaches the committee
The respondent is given the allegations in writing, promptly
The respondent submits a written response
The committee hears both sides and examines evidence and witnesses
The committee sends its findings and recommendations to the decision-maker
The decision-maker decides and applies any sanction
Either party appeals or uses an external route, if they wish and the law allows

cards.title: Outcomes and safeguards
cards.prompt: Match each term to what it means in a fair harassment process (paraphrased; check your local law).

pairs.right: Matched to the seriousness of what was found: from a written warning up to demotion or dismissal
Putting things right for the person harmed: restored opportunities, an apology or compensation
Action only where a complaint is found to be deliberately false; failing to prove a complaint is not the same
A party unhappy with the decision can ask for a review or go to an external body
Some laws, such as India's, fine organisations that fail duties such as forming a committee

cards.title: Zara asks what to do
cards.situation: Zara meets you at the plant. She is anxious: 'I want it to stop. I don't want to ruin his life, but I don't want to be the one who leaves. And his uncle is on the committee.' She asks what her options are. What do you do?

choices.text: Tell her the internal committee is the only route and she must file there today, or the company can't help.
choices.outcome: Zara feels cornered, given the uncle's seat. She delays, and the messages continue. Pushing a single route ignores her choice and the conflict of interest.

choices.text: Explain her options plainly: informal resolution, a formal complaint (the uncle stepping aside), outside routes such as the police; confidentiality; no retaliation; interim steps. Let her choose.
choices.outcome: Zara chooses a formal internal complaint once you confirm the uncle will step aside. She feels in control. The case starts fairly for both sides.

choices.text: Suggest she first talks to Victor herself and tells him firmly to stop.
choices.outcome: She has already done this twice. Asking her to confront him again puts the burden on her. Direct communication can be one informal option if she wants it, but not the advice by itself.

choices.text: Call Victor in yourself, warn him off and close the matter without a record.
choices.outcome: Victor guesses who complained and the messages stop, but the group members turn cold on Zara. No record, no process, no protection. If it happens again, there is nothing on file.

cards.title: Real case: from Vishaka to India's workplace law
cards.body:
In 1992 a grassroots social worker in Rajasthan, who had campaigned against child marriage, was sexually assaulted. Women's groups argued that India had no law protecting women from sexual harassment at work, and petitioned the Supreme Court.

- In **1997**, in *Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan*, the Court drew on CEDAW to set binding guidelines: employers had to prevent harassment and set up a complaints committee headed by a woman.
- Those guidelines applied for 16 years, until Parliament passed the **Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013**.
- The Act requires Internal Committees in workplaces with 10 or more employees, with district-level Local Committees for smaller workplaces. It also says that failing to prove a complaint is not, by itself, grounds for action against the complainant.

**Lesson:** international standards matter in practice. Courts and lawmakers use them to fill gaps in national law.

cards.title: Other laws that may apply
cards.body:
The workplace process is not the only route. The same conduct may also be:

- **A crime.** Sexual assault, stalking and some forms of harassment are criminal offences in most countries. Criminal complaints go to the police and courts, not the internal committee.
- **An online offence.** Many countries now criminalise cyberstalking and sharing intimate or faked sexual images without consent, for example Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 and offences added in the UK by the Online Safety Act 2023.
- **Discrimination** under equality or labour law, which can be taken to a tribunal or court.

These routes can run **alongside** the workplace process: one deals with employment consequences, the others with crimes or legal claims. Reporting channels change, so check the current ones where you work, and take legal advice for serious cases.

cards.question: Joseph says the 'Shift B' chat group isn't covered because it is on personal phones. What is the best answer?
options: He is right; only conduct inside the plant building counts
It is covered only if the company pays for the phones
It can only be dealt with by the police, not the company
Work-related messaging among colleagues is in scope under C190 and most policies, and online-abuse laws may also apply to the edited image
cards.explanation: ILO Convention 190 covers work-related communications, and a group of colleagues organised around shifts is work-related. Sharing an edited image may also be an offence under online-abuse laws. The company process and criminal routes can run in parallel.

cards.title: Check the rules where you work, every time
cards.body:
This stage gives the international standard and examples from several countries. Your duties depend on where each person works, and laws, court rulings and reporting channels change.

- Keep the **current** law for every country (and state or province) where you operate.
- Don't copy another country's procedure: committee make-up, time limits and external routes differ.
- Ask your legal team which external bodies apply.
- Write time limits into your procedure and track them in a case log.
- When in doubt, get advice before a deadline passes, not after.

cards.title: Code Wall scaled
items: ILO Convention 190 (2019, in force 2021) is the first global treaty on violence and harassment at work, and it includes gender-based harassment.
It protects people whatever their contract, including interns, volunteers and job seekers, and covers trips, events, work messages and the commute.
Laws follow three broad models: harassment as discrimination (US, UK, EU), dedicated laws with internal committees (India, Pakistan) and duties to prevent (Australia, UK).
Employers need a policy made with workers, risk assessment, visible rules, a trained and gender-balanced committee, and protection from retaliation.
A fair inquiry gives the respondent the allegations promptly, hears both sides and ends in proportionate outcomes with appeal or an external route; unproven is not false.
Criminal and online-abuse laws can run in parallel. Always check the rules where you work.

cards.prompt: Do you know who sits on your organisation's harassment committee, which law applies where you work, and which outside bodies people can go to? If someone came to you tomorrow, could you explain their options in two minutes? Write down what you would need to find out.

quiz.question: Which treaty, adopted in 2019, is the first international treaty on violence and harassment in the world of work?
options: ILO Convention 190
CEDAW, the UN women's rights convention
ILO Convention 100
ILO Convention 183
quiz.explanation: ILO Convention 190 (2019, in force 2021) is the first international treaty on violence and harassment at work. CEDAW (1979) is the UN women's rights convention; Conventions 100 and 183 cover equal pay and maternity.

quiz.question: Under ILO Convention 190, who is protected from violence and harassment at work?
options: Only employees on permanent contracts with the organisation itself, not interns or volunteers
Only women, as the main targets of harassment
People working whatever their contract, including interns, volunteers and job seekers
Only staff who have completed their probation period
quiz.explanation: C190 protects people whatever their contractual status, including interns, apprentices, volunteers, job seekers and people whose job has ended. It is not limited to women or to permanent staff.

quiz.question: What did the US Supreme Court decide in Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson (1986)?
options: That harassment only counts if it involves physical contact
That a hostile working environment is sex discrimination, even with no lost pay or promotion
That employers are never responsible for what their supervisors do
That only 'do this or else' harassment, where pay or promotion is directly at stake, is unlawful
quiz.explanation: Meritor recognised hostile-environment harassment as sex discrimination under the Civil Rights Act 1964, even with no economic loss. It also made 'unwelcome', not 'voluntary', the key test.

quiz.question: Under ILO Convention 190, which of these are employers expected to do?
options: Keep the harassment policy confidential within HR
Wait for staff to report specific risks to their managers before taking any preventive action
Act only once a formal complaint has been made
Adopt a policy with workers, assess the risks, and inform and train staff
quiz.explanation: C190 expects employers to adopt a policy in consultation with workers, include the risks in health and safety management, assess hazards and provide information and training. Waiting for complaints is not prevention.

quiz.question: A clerk does not trust her company's internal committee because the person she wants to complain about is her director. What is generally true?
options: She has no option but the internal committee
She can only resign first and then bring a claim for damages against the company through the courts
Depending on the country, an outside route: an ombudsperson, tribunal or the police
She must ask the director's permission before going outside
quiz.explanation: Most systems offer routes outside the organisation: an ombudsperson in Pakistan, tribunals in the UK, the EEOC in the US, and the police for crimes. Which ones apply depends on the country.

quiz.question: Once a written complaint reaches the committee, what is the next step in a fair inquiry?
options: The decision-maker immediately applies a sanction
The respondent is given the allegations in writing, promptly
The complaint is sent to the police for investigation
The complainant is asked to withdraw and try informal resolution first
quiz.explanation: The respondent must promptly receive the allegations in writing so they can respond. Sanctions come only after findings, and the police route is separate.

quiz.question: Which of these is a remedy for the person harassed, rather than a sanction on the respondent?
options: A final written warning kept on the respondent's personnel file
Demotion
Dismissal
Restoring a lost opportunity and offering compensation
quiz.explanation: A remedy puts things right for the person harmed, for example restoring an opportunity, an apology or compensation. Warnings, demotion and dismissal are sanctions on the respondent, matched to seriousness.

quiz.question: The committee finds there is not enough evidence to prove a complaint, but nothing suggests the complainant lied. What follows?
options: The complaint is not proved, but this does not make it a false complaint deserving action
The complainant must be penalised for a false complaint
The case automatically goes to the police
The respondent must still receive at least a warning, since the complaint was not withdrawn
quiz.explanation: Action against a complainant is only for complaints found to be deliberately false. India's 2013 Act says so expressly. Punishing unproven complaints would deter genuine reports.

quiz.question: A colleague circulates an edited, sexualised image of a female co-worker in a work chat group. Besides the workplace route, what may also apply?
options: Company law on directors' duties, board reporting and shareholder rights
Consumer protection rules on digital services
Criminal or online-abuse laws on sharing intimate or faked images
Only health and safety regulations, not other laws
quiz.explanation: Many countries criminalise sharing intimate or faked sexual images without consent, for example in Pakistan and the UK. That route can run alongside the workplace process.

quiz.question: Who usually decides any sanction after a harassment committee completes its findings?
options: The committee chair, acting alone
A senior decision-maker the organisation designates in its procedure
The complainant, who chooses the sanction she considers fair in the circumstances
The local police station
quiz.explanation: The committee sends findings and recommendations to a designated decision-maker, who decides and applies any sanction. Either party can then appeal or use an external route.

sessions.title: Recognise, Respond, Step In: Harassment in Real Life
sessions.summary: Turn the rules into action. Recognise harassment in person and in group chats, respond well when someone confides in you, protect people from retaliation, step in safely as a bystander, and practise everyday allyship, especially as a man, in meetings and beyond.
objectives: Recognise the range of harassing behaviour, including online and messaging-app patterns, using impact rather than intent
Respond to a disclosure as a colleague or manager in a way that is supportive, fair and procedurally sound
Preserve evidence of online harassment correctly
Use the five Ds of bystander intervention and recognise retaliation
Practise allyship and run inclusive meetings

cards.title: The silence after
cards.setting: Plant canteen, Thika. Two weeks after Zara's complaint. Lunch break.

lines.text: The inquiry is under way. Victor has been moved to a different shift while it runs. But something else is happening.
Nobody sits with me now. The Shift B group was deleted and a new one made. I wasn't added. My line data 'goes missing' before reviews.
I need to tell you something, Leila. I was in that group. I saw the photo the day it was posted. I didn't say anything.
Thank you for saying it, Joseph. Most people stay silent because they don't know what to do, not because they agree.
But what's happening to Zara now has a name: retaliation. And silence from twenty-six people helped it start.
Stage four is the Bystander Bridge. Let's learn to see it early, respond well and step in, without making things worse.

scenes.heading: The question is how it lands
scenes.narration: Harassment is judged by whether conduct is unwelcome and what it does to the person, not by whether the sender 'meant well' or 'was only joking'.

scenes.heading: Silence is not consent
scenes.narration: Many people don't object out loud, especially to a supervisor who controls their shifts or appraisal. Not saying no is not the same as saying yes.

scenes.heading: The phone is part of work
scenes.narration: Late-night personal messages, comments on someone's profile photo, unsolicited images or voice notes, pressure for video calls: in chat apps the pattern is often persistence after no reply.

scenes.heading: Small things build walls
scenes.narration: Jokes, nicknames and exclusion seem minor alone. Tolerated, they create a climate where bigger harms feel normal.

scenes.heading: Look for the pattern
scenes.narration: Ask three questions: is it unwelcome, is it about gender or sexual in nature, and is it affecting the person's work or sense of safety?

cards.title: Why silence is the default
cards.caption: Real survey and regulator figures, rounded. They show why bystanders and managers have to make speaking up safe.

items.label: Harassed or abused at work
items.detail: First global survey by the ILO with Lloyd's Register Foundation and Gallup (2022): people in work who had faced violence or harassment at some point.

items.label: Never told a manager
items.detail: US EEOC task force (2016): most people who experience harassment never report it to a supervisor, manager or union representative.

items.label: Top issue in US charges
items.detail: Since 2010, retaliation has been the most frequently alleged issue in charges filed with the US EEOC.

items.label: UK women harassed at work
items.detail: A 2016 UK survey by the Trades Union Congress found 52% of women had experienced sexual harassment at work.

cards.title: How harm escalates
cards.caption: The top rests on the base. When the everyday layers are tolerated, the serious ones become more likely.

items.label: Assault and coercion
items.detail: Physical assault, sexual coercion: criminal matters as well as workplace ones.

items.label: Threats and 'comply or else'
items.detail: Linking shifts, confirmation or promotion to going along.

items.label: Unwanted touch and images
items.detail: Touching, sending or sharing sexual or edited images.

items.label: Persistent messages and comments
items.detail: Repeated late-night messages, remarks about looks or private life.

items.label: Jokes, stereotypes, exclusion
items.detail: Sexist 'banter', nicknames, leaving people out of groups and meetings.

cards.title: Chat apps: red flag or professional?
cards.prompt: Sort each message pattern from Saffron Line staff phones.

items.text: 'Your profile picture is looking very nice today 😉' from a supervisor at 1 am
'Line 3 down, can you check the oven log?' sent at 11 pm during a night trial
Repeated 'why aren't you replying?' after no response
A forwarded edited photo of a colleague with a joke caption
A team group reminder about tomorrow's 9 am audit
Adding a colleague to a private 'fun' group without asking, then sending personal voice notes
'Thanks for covering today, appreciated' after a shift swap
Asking a junior to switch to video call 'to talk privately' about nothing work-related

cards.question: A supervisor says his messages to a trainee were 'just friendly' and he 'meant no harm'. She has not replied to most of them and has asked a colleague to swap shifts to avoid him. Which factor matters most?
options: His intention, since he says he meant no harm
Whether she ever told him 'no' in writing
Whether the messages were sent on a company phone
Whether the conduct is unwelcome and its impact on her work and safety
cards.explanation: Harassment is judged on whether conduct is unwelcome and its effect, not on stated intent. Her silence and shift swaps are signs it is unwelcome. A written 'no' is not required, and the device does not decide it.

cards.title: When someone confides in you
cards.caption: Whether you are a colleague or a manager, how you respond in the first ten minutes shapes whether they ever speak up again.

items.label: Listen without judging
items.detail: Let them speak. Don't interrupt, interrogate or ask 'why didn't you…?'.

items.label: Thank and reassure
items.detail: 'Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing.'

items.label: Be honest on confidentiality
items.detail: Promise discretion and need-to-know sharing, not total secrecy.

items.label: Explain the options
items.detail: Informal resolution, the internal committee, external bodies and other legal routes.

items.label: Ask what they need
items.detail: Safety, shift changes, leave, support. Act with their consent where possible.

items.label: Refer, record, follow up
items.detail: Refer to the committee or HR, note facts and dates, check in later. Don't investigate yourself.

cards.title: Preserving online evidence
cards.prompt: Zara's friend at another plant receives harassing messages. Put the evidence steps in the best order.
steps: Don't delete or reply angrily; leave the messages in place
Take screenshots showing the sender's number or name, date and time
Export or back up the chat and save copies somewhere secure
Write a short note of what happened, when, and who else saw it
Take the evidence to the harassment committee or HR
If an online offence may be involved, consider reporting it to the police or cybercrime unit

cards.title: The distributor dinner
