cards.setting: A hotel restaurant in Kuala Lumpur. Saffron Line's annual South-East Asia distributor dinner. Joseph is visiting for a supply review.

lines.text: A large distributor, Mr Voss, has had Mei Ling seated next to him. His comments have drifted from targets to her appearance.
(quietly, to Joseph at the buffet) He's put his hand on my chair twice and asked if my husband 'lets me' travel. I need this account.
Then let's not leave you alone with it. Give me one minute.
(at the table) Mr Voss, I've been meaning to ask about your Penang warehouse. Mei Ling, would you take my seat so we can talk shop?
(later) Thank you. That was smooth. But I don't want this to happen at the next dinner either.
Agreed. I'll back you when you raise it with Graham, and the account plan can't depend on you sitting next to him.

cards.title: The five Ds of stepping in

cards.back: Name it calmly: 'That's not okay, please stop.' Best when you feel safe and it won't escalate the danger.
Interrupt the moment indirectly: a question, a spilt drink, 'Mei Ling, the boss is calling you'. Low risk, often very effective.
Get help from someone with more authority or skill: a manager, security, HR or a committee member.
If you couldn't act in the moment, check in afterwards: 'I saw that. Are you okay? What would help?'
Note or screenshot what happened, then give it to the person affected. Never share it around or post it without their consent.

cards.title: The meme in the group
cards.situation: In the 'Singapore Sales Team' chat group (34 members, including two managers), a colleague posts a meme mocking 'lady drivers' with a photo of Nurul, a new sales officer, edited onto it. Three people react with laughing emojis. Nurul is in the group and goes silent. You are a peer, not a manager. What do you do?

choices.text: Ignore it; reacting will only make it a bigger deal for Nurul.
choices.outcome: The meme stays up. Two more 'jokes' follow that week. Nurul reads the silence as agreement and starts avoiding the team.

choices.text: Post a short, calm message ('Not funny, let's keep this group professional') and message Nurul privately to check she's okay and ask what she'd like; save a screenshot for her if she wants to report it.
choices.outcome: The poster deletes the meme. One of the managers adds 'Agreed'. Nurul thanks you, and decides to raise it informally with her manager with your screenshot. Direct, delay and document, used together.

choices.text: Forward the screenshot to the wider company group so everyone sees how bad the poster is.
choices.outcome: Now Nurul's edited photo has been seen by 300 more people. Spreading the image harms the person you meant to help. Documenting means giving evidence to her, not broadcasting it.

choices.text: Message the poster privately to say it's not okay, but say nothing to Nurul.
choices.outcome: The poster deletes it, which helps. But Nurul never learns anyone noticed, and doesn't know she has support or options if it happens again.

cards.title: Retaliation: the second harm
cards.body:
**Retaliation** is any negative treatment of someone because they complained, supported a complaint or gave evidence. It can be more damaging than the original conduct, because it tells everyone what happens to people who speak up.

Watch for:
- Sudden poor ratings, missing data or 'performance concerns' after a complaint
- Being removed from groups, meetings, shifts or projects
- Rumours, cold-shouldering and 'jokes' about the complaint
- Pressure to withdraw or to 'settle it informally' for the team's sake

Managers have a duty to stop it. Treat retaliation as **serious misconduct**, keep the complainant's work assessed on evidence, and keep details on a **need-to-know** basis. Interim steps, such as changing reporting lines or shifts, should not punish the complainant: move the accused where possible, and agree any change with the complainant first.

cards.title: Allyship in action
cards.prompt: Match each ally behaviour to an example from Saffron Line.

pairs.right: 'As Zara said ten minutes ago, the oven downtime fix is hers. Let's give her the floor.'
Graham puts Mei Ling's name forward for the Middle East role and vouches for her in the room.
Joseph takes paternity leave and leaves at 5 pm on Tuesdays for the school pick-up.
'Mate, that comment about her husband was out of line. Let's not.'
Asking Mei Ling what support she wants before acting, instead of 'rescuing' her.

cards.title: Performative or real allyship?
cards.caption: Allyship is measured by what changes for the other person, not by how supportive the ally looks.

items.label: Visibility
items.left: Posts on International Women's Day, silent the rest of the year
items.right: Speaks up in the meeting where it matters

items.label: Credit
items.left: Repeats a woman's idea as his own
items.right: Names who had the idea first

items.label: Help
items.left: Decides what she needs and 'rescues' her
items.right: Asks what she wants and follows her lead

items.label: Care work
items.left: Praises mothers in speeches
items.right: Takes his own leave and covers fairly

cards.title: Running an inclusive meeting
cards.body:
- **Timing**: schedule key meetings in working hours, not 7 pm 'quick catch-ups'.
- **Rotate the chores**: note-taking, tea and booking rooms are not one person's job.
- **Stop interruptions**: 'Hold on, Zara was mid-point.'
- **Credit by name**: record who raised which idea in the minutes.
- **Bring in quiet voices**: go round the table or invite written input before the meeting.
- **Hybrid fairness**: call on remote participants first sometimes.
- **Venues**: choose places all staff can attend safely and comfortably.

cards.question: A manager tells a complainant: 'While the inquiry runs, it's better if you work from the warehouse office so things stay calm.' She did not ask for this and loses her sales territory. What is the main problem?
options: Nothing; separating the parties is always correct
The interim step punishes the complainant and may be retaliation; the accused should be moved where possible, with her agreement on any change
The manager should have moved both of them to the warehouse
The manager should have waited until the inquiry ended before doing anything
cards.explanation: Separating the parties can be right, but the complainant should not bear the cost. Moving her against her wishes and taking her territory signals punishment for complaining.

cards.title: Real case: Uber's 2017 reckoning
cards.body:
In February 2017 Susan Fowler, a former Uber engineer, published a blog post about her year at the company.

- She described reporting her manager's sexual propositions to HR, being told it was his first offence, and being offered a move to another team. She said she later learned other women had reported the same manager.
- Uber asked former US Attorney General Eric Holder's law firm to review its culture and practices; its recommendations, published in June 2017, covered HR, complaint handling and leadership accountability.
- A separate review of complaints led to more than 20 people being fired, and chief executive Travis Kalanick resigned in June 2017.

**Lessons:** treating each report as a 'first offence' hides patterns. Moving the complainant, not the accused, punishes the person who spoke up. And a culture of silence eventually becomes a crisis for everyone.

cards.title: How Joseph changed the plant
cards.body:
After admitting he stayed silent, Joseph made four changes at Thika:

1. **Groups**: work chat groups now have a pinned rule (work only, no images of colleagues) and two admins, one of them a woman.
2. **Shift briefings**: every briefing ends by naming one committee member people can approach, including a woman member.
3. **Retaliation watch**: for six months after any complaint, Joseph personally reviews the complainant's ratings and shift allocations for sudden changes.
4. **Men talking to men**: he raised the group photo at a supervisors' meeting himself: 'I saw it and said nothing. That was wrong. From now on, we say something.'

The fourth change mattered most. Coming from the plant manager, it made speaking up normal.

cards.title: Bystander Bridge crossed
items: Harassment is judged by whether conduct is unwelcome and its impact, not intent; silence is not consent.
In chat apps, look for persistence after no reply, comments on looks, unsolicited or edited images and pressure for private calls.
When someone confides: listen, thank, be honest about confidentiality, explain options, ask what they need, refer and follow up; don't investigate yourself.
Preserve evidence: don't delete, screenshot with sender, date and time, back up, note witnesses.
The five Ds: Direct, Distract, Delegate, Delay, Document; give documentation to the person affected, never spread it.
Retaliation is serious misconduct; real allies amplify, sponsor, share care and call in other men.
Most harassment is never reported and retaliation is common, so check for patterns across reports and never make the complainant pay the price, as Uber's 2017 crisis showed.

cards.prompt: Recall a moment when you saw a gendered joke, comment or message and said nothing. Which of the five Ds could you realistically have used? Write the exact words you would say next time.

quiz.question: When deciding whether conduct may be harassment, which question matters most?
options: Did the person intend to cause offence?
Was it said inside the office building?
Did the target object loudly at the time?
Is it unwelcome, and what effect is it having on the person's work or safety?
quiz.explanation: Harassment turns on whether conduct is unwelcome and its impact. Intent, location inside the building and a loud objection are not the test.

quiz.question: Which chat-app pattern is the clearest red flag?
options: A night-shift supervisor messaging an engineer at 11 pm about a machine fault
A supervisor repeatedly asking a junior 'why aren't you replying?' about personal messages after she stops responding
A team group reminder about tomorrow's audit
A thank-you note after a colleague covers a shift
quiz.explanation: Persistence after no reply, from someone with power over the target, is a classic red flag. A late message about a real work issue on a night trial is professional.

quiz.question: A colleague tells you a manager has been touching her shoulder and making comments about her clothes. She asks you to keep it 'completely secret'. What is the best reply?
options: Promise discretion, but explain you can't promise total secrecy if action is needed, then go through her options
Promise total secrecy so she keeps trusting you
Tell her you must report it to her manager's boss straight away, whatever she wants, because that is the only safe option
Tell her to keep a low profile until the manager is transferred
quiz.explanation: Be honest: you can be discreet but may not be able to keep everything secret, especially where there is a risk to her or others. Then explain options and, where possible, act with her consent.

quiz.question: A team leader receives a disclosure of harassment against a peer. Which action should he avoid?
options: Thanking the person for speaking up
Explaining the internal and external complaint routes
Calling the accused into his office to question him about the allegations
Writing down the facts and dates he was told
quiz.explanation: Investigating or confronting the accused yourself can compromise the process, alert the accused and expose the complainant. Refer to the committee, which will give the accused a fair hearing.

quiz.question: Which is the first step in preserving evidence of harassing messages?
options: Leave the messages in place rather than deleting them or replying angrily
Forward them to the whole team so there are many witnesses
Block and delete the chat immediately
Post the messages publicly so the sender is shamed
quiz.explanation: Keep the original messages, then screenshot with sender, date and time and back up the chat. Deleting loses evidence; sharing widely spreads the harm.

quiz.question: At a client lunch, a client keeps making remarks about a young officer's appearance. A colleague says, 'Ama, the office is calling about the Jakarta order, can you step out?' Which of the five Ds is this?
options: Direct
Delegate
Document
Distract
quiz.explanation: Distract interrupts the situation indirectly without confrontation. Direct would name the behaviour; Delegate would bring in someone with more authority.

quiz.question: You witnessed a sexist remark in a meeting but couldn't respond at the time. What does 'Delay' mean in the five Ds?
options: Waiting a month to see if it happens again before deciding
Checking in with the person afterwards to see if they are okay and what would help
Asking the speaker, politely, to delay any further comments of that kind until after the meeting has ended
Postponing the meeting
quiz.explanation: Delay is checking in afterwards, which reduces isolation and opens the way to further support. It is not waiting to see whether harm repeats.

quiz.question: After filing a complaint, an officer finds her name removed from the monthly review meeting invite and her figures 'lost' before appraisals. What is this most likely to be?
options: Normal administrative error that needs no attention
A performance issue the officer must address
Retaliation, which managers should treat as serious misconduct
An approved interim measure under the policy
quiz.explanation: Exclusion and sudden data problems right after a complaint are typical signs of retaliation. Managers must stop it and keep her assessment evidence-based.

quiz.question: In a meeting, a male manager says: 'As Sofia said earlier, let's go with her pricing idea. Sofia, want to take us through it?' What ally behaviour is this?
options: Sponsorship
Delegation
Benevolent sexism
Amplification
quiz.explanation: Amplification gives credit by name and returns the floor to the person who had the idea. Sponsorship is using one's influence to advance someone's career, such as nominating them for a role.

quiz.question: As a bystander, you screenshot a harassing post in a group chat. What should you do with it?
options: Give it to the person affected and let them decide how to use it
Post it in another group to warn others
Send it straight to the poster's family
Keep it to yourself and do nothing else
quiz.explanation: Documentation belongs to the person affected, who decides whether to report. Spreading it multiplies the harm.

sessions.title: Careers, Inclusion and Measuring What Matters
sessions.summary: Bring it all together for the board. Diagnose the leaky pipeline and the broken rung, use sponsorship to move careers, welcome transgender colleagues with dignity, and measure progress with the right numbers, including how to calculate a pay gap and a promotion-rate ratio.
objectives: Diagnose where women leave the pipeline and explain the 'broken rung'
Distinguish mentoring from sponsorship and match interventions to pipeline barriers
Treat transgender colleagues with dignity, knowing that legal protection differs between countries and must be checked locally
Calculate and interpret a gender pay gap, promotion-rate ratio and attrition rates
Build a measurement cycle and present progress honestly to senior leaders

cards.title: Two weeks to the board
cards.setting: Strategy room, group head office, Dubai. A whiteboard full of numbers.

lines.text: Two weeks to the board. Here's our pipeline: women are 46% of graduate trainees, 40% of officers, 21% of first-line managers, 12% of senior managers, and one of eight on ExCo.
So it's a pipeline problem. Hire more women at the bottom and wait.
We've been hiring nearly half women at the bottom for a decade, Graham. The pipe isn't empty. It leaks.
(on video) And I nearly leaked out last year. What kept me was someone in the room saying my name.
One more thing. I'm covering the Nairobi customer-care centre this month. Amani, a transgender woman, has been hired there. The supervisors are nervous. They don't want to get it wrong.
Good. Nervous means they care. Final stage: the Summit Boardroom. Fix the leaks, welcome everyone, and prove it with numbers.

scenes.heading: In at the bottom, out along the way
scenes.narration: In many organisations women join in large numbers but thin out at each level. That pattern is called the leaky pipeline.

scenes.heading: The broken rung
scenes.narration: The biggest drop is often the very first step into management. Global workplace research calls it the broken rung. Miss that step and the senior pool never fills.

scenes.heading: Why women leave the pipe
scenes.narration: Bias in promotions, the maternal wall, late-evening culture, unsafe travel, harassment and fewer sponsors. It is rarely one reason, and rarely just 'marriage'.

scenes.heading: Fix the leak, not the women
scenes.narration: Training women to be 'more confident' doesn't fix a biased promotion panel. Change the process, the culture and who speaks up for whom.

scenes.heading: Measure each joint
scenes.narration: Track representation, promotion and exit rates at every level. The numbers tell you exactly which joint is leaking.

cards.title: Saffron Line's pipeline: share of women
cards.caption: Women's share at each level. Compare neighbouring levels to find the biggest leak.

cards.question: Using Saffron Line's pipeline (46% trainees, 40% officers, 21% first-line managers, 12% senior managers), where is the biggest drop in women's share between neighbouring levels?
options: Trainees to officers (6 points)
Officers to first-line managers (19 points)
First-line to senior managers (9 points)
There is no meaningful drop at any level
cards.explanation: 40% to 21% is a 19-point fall, much larger than 46 to 40 (6 points) or 21 to 12 (9 points). This is the 'broken rung': the first step into management.

cards.title: Mentor or sponsor?
cards.caption: Research on careers often finds women are well mentored but under-sponsored. Both help; sponsorship moves careers.

items.label: Role
items.left: Talks with you: advice and perspective
items.right: Talks about you: advocates when you're not in the room

items.label: Uses
items.left: Experience and time
items.right: Influence and reputation

items.label: Typical act
items.left: Reviews your CV, helps you prepare
items.right: Nominates you for a stretch role and vouches for you

items.label: Risk taken
items.left: Low
items.right: Real: their name is on your success

cards.title: Match the fix to the leak
cards.prompt: Each barrier was found in Saffron Line's data. Match it to the intervention that most directly addresses it.

pairs.left: Few women nominated for first-line manager roles
pairs.right: Structured, criteria-based nominations, plus senior sponsors for high-potential women

pairs.left: High exits in the year after maternity leave
pairs.right: Return-to-work programme, phased return and appraisal protection

pairs.left: Women decline field roles with late returns
pairs.right: Safe transport and travel policy, planned with the people affected

pairs.left: Ideas credited to whoever repeats them loudest
pairs.right: Inclusive meeting rules: credit by name in minutes

pairs.left: Exit interviews cite harassment and retaliation
pairs.right: Visible committee, bystander training and retaliation monitoring

cards.title: Amani's first day
cards.setting: Customer-care centre, Nairobi. Amani has been hired on merit after a structured interview. Joseph is covering for the centre head today.

lines.text: Leila, the team lead asked me which name to put on the system and the desk plate. The name on her ID and the name she uses are different.
Use the name and form of address she uses at work everywhere people see it. Keep official records accurate and private, on a need-to-know basis.
And the washrooms? Two of the team asked.
Ask Amani what she's comfortable with, and make sure there's a dignified option, like a single-user washroom anyone can use. Don't make her the subject of a staff debate.
(visiting for a training) And tell the team that the harassment policy covers her too. Jokes about her are not 'banter'.

cards.title: Transgender colleagues: respect in practice
cards.body:
**The law differs widely between countries and keeps changing**, so check the current position wherever you operate. For example:

- **US:** in *Bostock v. Clayton County* (2020) the Supreme Court held that firing someone for being transgender is sex discrimination.
- **UK:** the Equality Act 2010 protects 'gender reassignment'. In 2025 the Supreme Court ruled that 'sex' in the Act means biological sex, which affects single-sex spaces.
- **Pakistan:** a 2018 Act bars discrimination at work. In 2023 a religious court found parts of it contrary to Islamic injunctions; appeals were filed.

Whatever the law, the workplace basics hold:

- **Hire and promote on merit** against the same criteria.
- **Use the name and form of address** the person uses at work.
- **Protect privacy**: no questions about bodies, medical history or past names.
- **Facilities**: talk to the person and offer a dignified option, such as a single-user washroom, within local rules.
- **Harassment rules apply fully.** Mockery is misconduct.

cards.title: The question in the team huddle
cards.situation: In the morning huddle at the customer-care centre, a team member asks Amani in front of everyone: 'So are you a man or a woman? What's your real name?' A few people laugh. Amani looks down. You are the team lead. What do you do?

choices.text: Laugh it off and move to the day's targets, so it doesn't become awkward.
choices.outcome: The questioner takes the laughter as permission. By lunch there are nicknames. Amani hands in her notice within a month. Moving on signalled that the mockery was acceptable.

choices.text: Say calmly, 'That's personal and not okay to ask. Let's get on with the briefing.' Afterwards, check in privately with Amani, and speak to the team member about the code of conduct.
choices.outcome: The room goes quiet, then the briefing carries on. Amani thanks you later. The team member apologises. You protected her privacy without turning her into a topic.

choices.text: Invite Amani to explain her identity to the team so everyone understands.
choices.outcome: Well meant, but it puts her on the spot and makes her private life a team topic. Education can help, but it shouldn't be her burden or happen at her expense.

choices.text: Wait and raise it at her next appraisal to see how she is coping.
choices.outcome: Weeks of silence send the message that the team lead didn't see or didn't care. Harassment needs a prompt response, not an appraisal note.

cards.title: The measurement cycle
cards.caption: Measurement is a loop, not a one-off report. Each turn should show what changed and why.

items.label: Collect
items.detail: Sex-disaggregated data on hiring, promotion, pay, exits, leave and complaints.

items.label: Analyse
items.detail: Find the gaps and the joints where the pipeline leaks.

items.label: Set targets and actions
items.detail: Realistic targets with owners, budgets and dates.

items.label: Implement
items.detail: Change processes, policies and manager behaviour.

items.label: Review and report
items.detail: Report honestly to leadership and staff, then start again.

cards.title: Real numbers from around the world
cards.caption: Real studies and laws, rounded. Use them as context for your own data, and check the latest edition or current law.

items.label: Women promoted per 100 men
items.detail: First step to manager, in McKinsey and LeanIn.Org's Women in the Workplace studies (2022 and 2023): the broken rung.

items.label: Norway's board rule
items.detail: A 2003 law requires at least 40% of each sex on boards of public limited companies. Fully enforced from 2008.

items.label: Iceland's equal pay proof
items.detail: Iceland began requiring larger employers to get certified that they pay women and men equally for work of equal value.

items.label: EU pay transparency
items.detail: An EU directive requires pay-gap reporting by larger employers. Member states had until June 2026 to apply it: check national status.

cards.title: Three calculations you must get right
cards.body:
**1. Unadjusted pay gap** = (men's average pay − women's average pay) ÷ men's average pay × 100.
Example: men average USD 4,000 a month, women USD 3,400. Gap = 600 ÷ 4,000 = **15%**. Do the same with **medians** (the middle value), which are less distorted by a few very high salaries.

The unadjusted gap mostly reflects **who is in which jobs**. An **adjusted** gap compares like with like (same grade, role, experience) and shows unequal pay for similar work.

**2. Promotion-rate ratio** = women's promotion rate ÷ men's promotion rate.
Example: 6 of 40 eligible women promoted (15%), 18 of 90 men (20%). Ratio = 15 ÷ 20 = **0.75**. 1.0 means parity.

**3. Attrition rate** = leavers ÷ average headcount × 100.
Example: 8 of 40 women managers left (20%) against 9 of 90 men (10%): women leave at **twice** the rate.

cards.question: In the sales division, men's average monthly pay is USD 5,000 and women's is USD 4,250. What is the unadjusted average pay gap?
cards.explanation: (5,000 − 4,250) ÷ 5,000 = 750 ÷ 5,000 = 0.15, so 15%. Dividing by women's pay instead (750 ÷ 4,250 ≈ 17.6%) uses the wrong base.

cards.back: Women's share at each grade. Shows where the pipeline leaks.
Women's promotion rate divided by men's. Below 1.0 means women are promoted less often from the same eligible pool.
Exits of people the company wanted to keep, split by gender and level, with exit reasons.
Share of parents still employed 12 months after returning from maternity or paternity leave.
Unadjusted shows job segregation; adjusted shows unequal pay for similar work. Report both.
Number of complaints, time to resolve, outcomes and retaliation reports. More complaints can mean more trust, not more harassment.

cards.title: Activity or outcome?
cards.prompt: Graham wants to know which numbers show effort and which show results. Sort each measure.

items.text: Number of managers trained on bias
Women's share of first-line managers
Day-care partnership signed
Share of mothers still employed a year after return
Number of awareness sessions held
Median gender pay gap
Harassment committee members trained
Women's regretted attrition rate

cards.title: Real case: Britain's gender pay gap reporting (2017 on)
cards.body:
Since **2017**, employers in Great Britain with **250 or more employees** must publish their gender pay gap every year on a government website: mean and median gaps in hourly pay and in bonuses, and the share of women and men in each pay quarter.

- More than 10,000 employers reported in the first round in 2018, and most showed a gap in favour of men.
- Many of the largest gaps came from who does which job, not from unequal pay for the same job. The airline easyJet, for example, reported a median gap of about 50%, explaining that most of its highly paid pilots were men and most cabin crew were women.
- Employers can add a written explanation, and many use it to set out causes and actions.

**Lesson:** the unadjusted gap reveals who holds which jobs; a like-for-like comparison tests equal pay. Report both, include the median, and say what you will do about it.

cards.question: In the year after Saffron Line trained staff and publicised the code, harassment complaints rose from 2 to 7. A board member says, 'Training made things worse.' What is the best reply?
options: Agree, and suspend the training programme
Ignore complaint numbers, since they cannot be interpreted
Stop publicising the code so complaints fall again
More complaints can reflect greater trust in reporting; look at resolution time, outcomes, retaliation reports and survey data on feeling safe to speak up
cards.explanation: When people trust the process, previously hidden cases come forward. Interpret complaint counts alongside other indicators, rather than treating a rise as failure or hiding the process.

cards.title: Presenting to the board
cards.body:
- **Lead with your own data**, then use outside research as context, framed as correlation.
- **Show the leak**: one pipeline chart beats ten slides.
- **Pair each gap with an action**, an owner and a date.
- **Report activity and outcomes** separately, so effort isn't mistaken for results.
- **Protect privacy**: don't report groups so small that individuals can be identified.
- **Be honest about what didn't work.** Boards trust candour.

cards.title: The summit
cards.setting: Saffron Line boardroom, Dubai. Ninety days after the survey. Leila, Graham and you at the front.

lines.text: Ninety days ago I said women leave for family reasons. Our exit data said otherwise. I was wrong, and I'd rather say so here than lose another Mei Ling.

Our plan has five parts: criteria-based promotions with sponsors, flexible work open to all, late-shift transport, a trained committee with retaliation monitoring, and a measured scorecard every quarter.
(from the back) And as of Monday, Regional Head, Middle East. Here in Dubai. My daughter has already chosen her school.
The inquiry concluded, the process was fair to both sides, and I've just been confirmed as process engineer. I'm staying.
And the plant's new rule: we say something. Every time.
The board approved it. Mission Equal Footing complete, almost. One last challenge: prove you can do it all without me. The final exam awaits.

cards.title: Summit reached
items: The leaky pipeline thins women out at each level; the biggest leak is often the 'broken rung' into first-line management.
Fix processes and culture, not women: criteria-based promotion, sponsors, return-to-work support, safe transport and retaliation monitoring.
Mentors advise; sponsors use their influence to advocate. Women are often under-sponsored.
Treat transgender colleagues with dignity: merit, their name and form of address, privacy and a dignified facility option; laws differ by country, so check locally.
Pay gap = (men's average − women's average) ÷ men's average; promotion-rate ratio = women's rate ÷ men's; report mean and median, adjusted and unadjusted.
Measure in a cycle, separate activity from outcome, read complaint numbers carefully and protect small groups' privacy.
Countries increasingly require transparency: Britain's pay gap reporting since 2017, Norway's 40% board rule and the EU's 2023 pay transparency directive.

cards.prompt: If you had to present your team's or organisation's gender picture tomorrow, which three numbers would you show, where do you think the leak is, and whom could you sponsor this year?

quiz.question: What does the 'broken rung' refer to?
options: The lack of women on company boards
The large drop in women's representation at the first step into management
Women leaving the workforce after marriage
A gap in women's technical training
quiz.explanation: The broken rung is the first promotion into management, where women's share often falls most. If that step is missed, the senior pool never fills.

quiz.question: Which action is sponsorship rather than mentoring?
options: Reviewing a colleague's CV and giving feedback
Meeting monthly to discuss career goals
Nominating a colleague for a stretch role and vouching for her in the selection meeting
Recommending books on leadership
quiz.explanation: A sponsor uses influence and reputation to advocate for someone, often when they are not in the room. CV feedback, goal discussions and reading lists are mentoring.

quiz.question: A company's women officers leave at high rates in the year after maternity leave. Which intervention most directly addresses this leak?
options: Confidence training for women officers
Hiring more women graduates
A Women's Day celebration
A return-to-work programme with a phased return and protection of appraisals during leave
quiz.explanation: The leak is at return from leave, so a planned return and appraisal protection target it directly. More hiring or confidence training does not change the conditions on return.

quiz.question: A new colleague is a transgender woman. Which approach reflects good workplace practice?
options: Use the name and form of address she uses at work and keep personal and medical matters private
Ask her to explain her medical history to HR in confidence, so the team leader can brief the team properly
Use the name on her official ID everywhere until the team gets used to her
Hold a team meeting to agree which washroom she should use
quiz.explanation: Respect means using the name and form of address she uses, protecting privacy and discussing facilities with her, not about her. Official records can be accurate and kept need-to-know.

quiz.question: Men's average monthly pay in a division is USD 5,000 and women's is USD 4,000. What is the unadjusted average gender pay gap?
quiz.explanation: (5,000 − 4,000) ÷ 5,000 = 1,000 ÷ 5,000 = 0.20, so 20%. Dividing by women's pay (1,000 ÷ 4,000) gives 25%, which uses the wrong base.

quiz.question: Of 50 eligible women, 5 were promoted; of 100 eligible men, 20 were promoted. What is the promotion-rate ratio (women's rate ÷ men's rate)?
quiz.explanation: Women's rate is 5 ÷ 50 = 10%; men's is 20 ÷ 100 = 20%. Ratio = 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5, meaning women are promoted half as often from the eligible pool.

quiz.question: Why should an organisation report a median pay gap as well as a mean (average) gap?
options: Because the median is always larger and so more convincing
Because the law requires only the median
Because the median is less distorted by a small number of very high salaries
Because the mean cannot be calculated for monthly pay
quiz.explanation: The median is the middle value, so a few very high earners affect it less than the mean. Reporting both gives a fuller picture.

quiz.question: Which of these is an outcome measure rather than an activity measure?
options: Number of bias workshops held
Number of managers who attended training
A day-care partnership signed
Women's share of first-line managers
quiz.explanation: Representation at a level is a result. Workshops, attendance and a signed partnership are activities, useful but not proof of change.

quiz.question: What does an unadjusted gender pay gap mostly reflect?
options: Only unequal pay for identical work done by women and men in the same grade
Differences in who holds which jobs and grades, as well as any unequal pay
Differences in tax rates for men and women
Only differences in bonuses
quiz.explanation: The unadjusted gap compares all men and all women, so it mainly reflects job and grade distribution. The adjusted gap compares like with like to reveal unequal pay for similar work.

quiz.question: An HR team supports staff in the US, the UK and Pakistan. Which statement about legal protection for transgender employees is most accurate?
options: The law is the same everywhere, because international human rights conventions settle the question for every country that has signed them
Only the US offers any protection, so the team can ignore the other two countries
It differs: Bostock (2020) covers US staff, UK law protects gender reassignment, Pakistan's 2018 Act is partly under appeal
None of the three countries has any law on gender identity, so only company policy matters
quiz.explanation: Protection differs by country and changes: Bostock (2020) in the US, 'gender reassignment' in the UK Equality Act (with a 2025 ruling on the meaning of 'sex'), and Pakistan's 2018 Act, parts of which were ruled against in 2023 and appealed. The team must check each country.

bank.question: During a workforce planning meeting at a plant in Manila, a manager says: 'Women don't apply for machine-operator roles because they are naturally not mechanical.' Records show the job advert says 'strong young men wanted' and the plant has no women's washroom. What is the most accurate analysis?
options: The statement reflects a real sex-linked difference in mechanical aptitude, so the plant should keep recruiting only men for these roles
The low applications prove the manager's point, since women had equal chance to apply
The statement treats a gender expectation as biology, and the advert and facilities are shaping who applies
The issue is only the washroom; the advert wording is a matter of style
bank.explanation: Being 'mechanical' is not a biological trait; it is a gender expectation. The advert wording and missing facilities discourage women from applying, so low applications reflect the system, not ability. Fixing only the washroom ignores the advert's message.

bank.question: A regional manager rates a female officer 'below expectations' after one late report, saying it shows she 'can't balance home and work'. He ignores her best-in-region recovery rate. A male officer with two late reports is rated 'meets expectations'. Which combination of biases is most evident?
options: Confirmation bias and the maternal wall
Affinity bias and the halo effect
Prove-it-again and hostile sexism
Attribution bias and benevolent sexism
bank.explanation: He picks one fact that fits his belief about working mothers and ignores stronger contrary evidence (confirmation bias), and the belief itself is the maternal wall. There is no shared-background favouritism (affinity) and no protective framing (benevolent sexism).

bank.question: A head of department says: 'I'm not biased. I just promote whoever shows the most confidence in the room.' Which response best reflects the course?
options: Confidence is a neutral, observable criterion, so the process is fair as long as he applies it consistently to every candidate he sees
He should promote more women to balance the numbers, whatever their confidence
Confidence matters only in sales roles, so the issue is limited to that team
Confidence displays follow gender scripts; he should define the behaviours that matter and assess everyone on them
bank.explanation: Prescriptive norms reward men for self-promotion and penalise women for it, so 'confidence in the room' is a biased signal. The fix is defined, job-relevant criteria applied to everyone, not lowering the bar or balancing numbers regardless of merit.

bank.question: Hina, a production supervisor, has successfully led two plant shutdowns. Before a third, the panel says, 'Let's give it to Kamran this time; we need to be sure Hina can handle it.' Kamran has led none. Which bias is this?
options: Affinity bias
Prove-it-again bias
Attribution bias
Halo effect
bank.explanation: Hina must keep proving competence she has already shown, while Kamran is trusted on potential. That is prove-it-again bias. Attribution bias would explain away her past success as luck; here the panel simply discounts it.

bank.question: In a calibration meeting, a manager describes a male engineer as 'assertive' and a female engineer as 'abrasive' for very similar recorded behaviour in a client escalation. As the HR facilitator, what is the most effective intervention?
options: Let it pass, since each manager knows their own team best
Ask both managers to describe the specific behaviour, then apply one agreed standard to both engineers
Remove all behavioural comments from appraisals in future, so that only hard numbers such as targets and deadlines are rated
Raise the female engineer's rating to compensate
bank.explanation: Turning labels into concrete behaviour and applying one standard is the bias interrupter. Removing behaviour from appraisals throws away useful information, and raising one rating without evidence is not fair either.

bank.question: A bank's policy says branch managers must 'use discretion' on who closes the branch late. In practice women are never rostered for late closing, so they never earn the late-duty experience required for promotion to operations manager. What is the root issue?
options: Women prefer early shifts, so the outcome reflects choice
The late-duty promotion criterion is itself unlawful harassment and must be removed from the policy entirely
There is no issue because the policy itself is gender-neutral
Unstructured discretion lets a gender script block a promotion route; solve the real need, such as safe transport
bank.explanation: Unstructured discretion is where stereotypes operate. Keeping women off late duty 'protects' them out of promotion. The fix is to ask staff, solve the genuine safety issue and roster fairly. Neutral wording does not guarantee neutral outcomes.

bank.question: A male finance officer asks to leave at 5 pm twice a week to collect his children while his wife works a hospital shift. His manager says, 'Be a man, let your wife handle that.' What is the best analysis?
options: A prescriptive norm is being used against a man, and it reinforces the idea that care is women's work
The comment is acceptable because it is addressed to a man
It is a descriptive stereotype only, so it has no workplace effect
It is a sex-linked matter, because looking after young children is a biologically determined role for mothers
bank.explanation: 'Be a man' enforces a prescriptive script and punishes a man for breaking it. It also keeps care on women's shoulders, which feeds the barriers women face. Childcare by fathers is a social role, not a biological one.

bank.question: An interview panel asks the female candidate, 'How will you manage this role with a family?' and asks the male candidate, 'What would you change in your first 90 days?' What is the best fix for future interviews?
options: Ask the family question to the male candidates as well, so that every candidate is treated in exactly the same way
Stop interviewing and rely only on CVs and test scores
Ask every candidate the same structured, job-related questions, including about real requirements such as travel
Allow each panel member to choose questions that fit each candidate
bank.explanation: Structured, job-related questions for all candidates remove the opening for stereotypes. Asking everyone about family is still not job-related; ask everyone about real requirements such as travel. Free choice of questions is how the problem arose.

bank.question: After a year of bias training, a firm's shortlists for management are still about 90% men, though graduate intake is roughly half women. Which next step best follows the 'check the pattern' principle?
options: Repeat the same training, since awareness takes time
Assume women do not want management roles
Introduce a fixed rule that every management shortlist must be exactly half women, starting from the next promotion round
Review shortlisting data by gender at each step to find where women drop out, then fix that step's criteria or process
bank.explanation: Patterns across many decisions reveal bias that single decisions hide. Locating the step where women fall away lets you fix the cause. Repeating training without data, assuming preferences or imposing a rigid split without diagnosis do not address the cause.

bank.question: At an offsite, a male director introduces the team: 'And here's our lovely Saira, who keeps us all in line, and the brains of the operation, Adeel.' Saira and Adeel hold equal roles. What is the most constructive response from a colleague?
options: Say nothing; it was clearly meant warmly, and raising it at all, even privately, would embarrass the director and spoil a good team day
Later, tell the director privately that he described Saira by looks and Adeel by ability, and suggest using roles
Interrupt immediately and tell the room the director is sexist
Ask Saira to correct the director herself, since it was about her
bank.explanation: A calm, private word that names the specific language and offers a better alternative fixes the issue without humiliation. Silence lets it repeat, public accusation tends to cause defensiveness, and pushing it onto Saira places the burden on the person affected.

bank.question: A telecom's call centre runs night shifts. Management offers a free drop home to 'all female staff' on nights; men on the same shifts get nothing. A male agent who lives on an unsafe route complains. What is the best redesign?
options: Base eligibility on shift timing and route risk, open to any employee, while keeping safeguards such as safe drop order
Keep it women-only, since equity always means giving extra support to women, and men on night shifts can be expected to manage
Withdraw the drop entirely so that everyone is treated the same
Pay a transport allowance to men only to balance the cost
bank.explanation: Equity targets the barrier (late shift on a risky route), not gender as a label. Women may still be the main beneficiaries, but anyone facing the same risk is covered. Withdrawing it fixes nothing and harms everyone.

bank.question: A CFO says: 'Gender inclusion is a cost centre. Show me one number.' You have the company's exit data: 9 regretted manager resignations last year, 6 of them women, each replaced after about four months of vacancy plus agency fees. What is the strongest opening for your case?
options: Quote a global consultancy study showing diverse companies are more profitable, and present it to the CFO as proof of the return
Argue that inclusion is the right thing to do, so cost does not matter
Promise that inclusion will raise profits by a specific percentage next year
Estimate the company's own replacement cost for these resignations and show which causes inclusion measures could address
bank.explanation: The company's own replacement cost is concrete and credible. Global studies support the case but show correlation, so they should not be presented as proof. Rights arguments matter but do not answer the CFO's question, and promised percentages overclaim.

bank.question: A public agency's selection committee informally prefers men for officer posts 'because the job involves field visits'. A qualified woman is rejected without being assessed. Which international standard is most directly engaged?
options: ILO Convention 183, because it sets out maternity protection for women
ILO Convention 111, which bars discrimination on the basis of sex in access to jobs
ILO Convention 190, because any unfair treatment of a woman at work counts as harassment
ILO Convention 100, because it guarantees equal pay for equal value
bank.explanation: Convention 111 covers discrimination, including on the basis of sex, in access to employment, training and conditions of work: rejecting a qualified woman unassessed is exactly that. Convention 100 concerns pay and Convention 183 maternity; C190 covers harassment, not every selection decision.

bank.question: A manager objects: 'A late-shift drop service designed for women breaches equality, because it treats people differently by sex.' What is the most accurate reply, based on CEDAW?
options: He is right; CEDAW requires identical treatment of women and men in every case
CEDAW binds only governments, so it says nothing useful about a private company's transport arrangements
CEDAW says temporary special measures to speed up real equality are not discrimination
CEDAW deals only with political rights, not with work
bank.explanation: CEDAW treats temporary special measures that accelerate real equality as non-discriminatory, so a protective measure can fit the principle. Designing it around actual risk rather than gender as a label is still better practice, as the night-shift case shows.

bank.question: Which statement for a board slide is best framed?
options: ILO estimates put women's labour force participation worldwide at just under half, against over 70% for men
Women's participation is the lowest it has ever been and will never change unless the board approves our programme
Diversity always produces higher profit, as proven by every global study
Women make up 70% of our customers, so they should make up 70% of our managers
bank.explanation: It gives a well-established figure attributed in general terms, without overclaiming. The others use absolute claims ('always', 'never', 'lowest ever') or unsupported numbers.

bank.question: A regional bank introduces flexible hours. Six months later, all 11 users are women, and two have been told in appraisals they 'lack commitment'. What should HR do first?
options: Close the scheme for now, because the appraisal comments show it is harming the careers of the women who use it
Restrict the scheme to women with children under five
Judge performance on output in appraisals and actively encourage all staff, including men, to use the scheme
Ask users to sign a waiver accepting slower promotion
bank.explanation: The policy is being penalised through appraisals and has become a 'mothers' scheme'. Judging output and normalising use by everyone fixes both. Closing it or adding waivers punishes the people it was meant to help.

bank.question: Arjun fears that approving one flexible-work request will 'open the floodgates'. Which approach best balances fairness and business needs?
options: Approve only requests from staff with the highest ratings
Approve requests informally and confidentially, case by case
Approve requests only for childcare reasons, since those are the most important and the easiest for colleagues to accept
Assess every request against the role's needs using the same criteria, with output measures and a review date
bank.explanation: Consistent criteria, output measures and review dates make decisions fair and manageable. Informal deals breed resentment, ranking reasons by 'importance' is arbitrary, and tying flexibility to ratings excludes people without a role-based reason.

bank.question: A company in India employs 120 people and has no childcare arrangement. A manager says, 'A crèche is a nice-to-have perk.' What is the most accurate response?
options: He is right; no country's labour law has ever mentioned childcare, so a crèche is purely a perk for well-funded firms
Since 2017 Indian law has required a crèche where there are 50 or more employees; check the current rules
A crèche is required in every organisation in every country, regardless of size
Childcare should be offered to women only, since men do not need it
bank.explanation: India's 2017 maternity benefit amendment requires establishments with 50 or more employees to provide a crèche facility, so it is a legal duty here, not a perk. Claiming no law exists, or that every organisation everywhere must run a crèche, are both inaccurate. Support should be open to fathers too.

bank.question: A plant offers paternity leave but none of the 300 male workers have taken it; supervisors joke about 'baby leave'. Which action is most likely to change uptake?
options: Have senior men take the leave visibly, brief supervisors that mocking it is unacceptable, and make it simple to apply
Send a reminder email that the policy exists
Make paternity leave compulsory for all fathers with immediate effect, with disciplinary action for any man who does not take it
Remove the policy, since there is no demand
bank.explanation: Uptake is blocked by a gender norm and ridicule, so role models, clear supervisor expectations and easy access address the actual barrier. A reminder email does not change the cost of using it.

bank.question: During a workshop, a participant says: 'Equity means women get promoted with lower scores.' Which correction is most accurate?
options: Correct; equity accepts lower scores temporarily so that representation targets can be reached sooner
Correct, but only in public-sector organisations
Incorrect; equity removes barriers to opportunity while everyone is held to the same standard
Incorrect; equity means everyone receives identical treatment
bank.explanation: Equity adjusts support, such as sponsorship, transport or flexible arrangements, not standards. Identical treatment describes equality, not equity.

bank.question: A logistics firm with 400 staff operates in a country whose law, like India's, requires employers to set up a harassment committee. It has a policy buried in its HR manual but no committee, and staff do not know how to complain. A driver's assistant wants to complain about a dispatcher. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: The firm is compliant because it has a written policy
Her complaint must wait until HR decides whether a committee is worth setting up, however long that takes
Only the police can now deal with the complaint
It is failing its duties: a policy on paper is not enough, and it must set up the committee
bank.explanation: Where the law requires a committee, a policy in a manual does not meet the duty, and laws such as India's allow fines for non-compliance. Her complaint should not be parked; the police route exists only for crimes and does not replace the workplace process.

bank.question: A woman engineer complains that her manager deliberately excludes her from all site assignments and promotion-relevant projects, saying 'the field is for men'. There is no sexual conduct. Is this within scope?
options: No; harassment rules only ever cover conduct of a sexual nature
Yes, it can be: C190 covers gender-based harassment, and Pakistan's 2022 amendment covers gender discrimination
No; it is only a performance matter, to be raised with the manager's own boss through the normal grievance route
Only if she also reports it to the police
bank.explanation: ILO Convention 190 expressly includes gender-based harassment, and Pakistan's 2022 amendment brought discrimination on the basis of gender within its harassment law. Elsewhere it may also be sex discrimination. Sexual conduct is not required.

bank.question: A complaint is filed against a sales manager whose brother-in-law is one of the three members of the harassment committee. What should the organisation do?
options: The related member steps aside and a replacement keeps the committee's required make-up, such as gender balance
Proceed as normal, recording the relationship in the file; the other two members can always outvote him if needed
Ask the complainant to accept the committee as it is or withdraw
Suspend the inquiry until the brother-in-law's term ends
bank.explanation: A member with a conflict of interest should step aside, and a substitute keeps the committee properly constituted. Proceeding or delaying undermines fairness, and the complainant may also have external routes.

bank.question: A harassment committee receives a complaint on 3 March. On 25 March it still has not given the respondent the allegations in writing, because members 'were busy with year-end'. What is the main problem?
options: None; the committee can set its own pace
The complaint has now expired under the usual time limits and must be dismissed, though she may file it again later
The allegations were due promptly; the delay is a process failure that weakens fairness for both sides
The complainant should have gone to the police instead
bank.explanation: A fair process gives the respondent the allegations promptly, and many laws, such as India's, set short time limits. Missing them is a process failure that harms both parties; it does not by itself extinguish the complaint.

bank.question: After an inquiry, the decision-maker gives the respondent only an informal word, despite strong evidence of repeated harassment. The complainant believes the outcome is far too light. What can she do?
options: Nothing; once the decision-maker has decided, the matter is closed for both parties for good, with no review
File a fresh, identical complaint with the same committee
Ask the committee to impose a second sanction itself
Use the appeal or external route available, such as an ombudsperson or tribunal, depending on the country
bank.explanation: A party unhappy with the decision can seek review through the internal appeal or an external body where the law allows, such as an ombudsperson or a tribunal. Refiling the same complaint is not the route, and the committee does not impose sanctions.

bank.question: The committee finds that a manager sent repeated sexual messages to a junior after she asked him to stop. He has no previous record. Which outcome best reflects proportionate sanctions and a remedy?
options: A sanction matched to seriousness, from final warning to dismissal, plus protection of her role
An informal chat, since it is his first recorded offence
Moving the junior to another team so that they no longer meet
Setting the findings aside, because a first offence by someone with a clean record should never lead to any sanction
bank.explanation: Repeated conduct after a clear 'stop' is serious, so a proportionate sanction is a significant one, alongside a remedy protecting the complainant. An informal chat understates it, and moving the complainant punishes her.

bank.question: A committee concludes that a complaint was fabricated to block a rival's promotion; messages show the complainant planned it with a colleague. What may the committee do?
options: Nothing; complainants are always protected regardless of intent, because any action would discourage other genuine reports
Recommend action against the complainant, as the complaint was found deliberately false
Refer the complainant to an ombudsperson for prosecution
Sanction the respondent anyway, to be safe
bank.explanation: Laws and good policies allow action where a complaint is found to be deliberately false. This is different from a complaint that simply cannot be proved, which must not be punished.

bank.question: A woman officer reports that a colleague has been sharing her photos with sexual captions in a private group of colleagues and sending her threats. She asks whether reporting to the police means she cannot also complain at work. What is the best answer?
options: She must choose one route only
The workplace route must be completed first, and only then can a police complaint be made about the same conduct
The police route replaces the workplace route because it is criminal
The routes can run in parallel: a workplace complaint and a criminal or online-abuse complaint
bank.explanation: Workplace, criminal and online-abuse routes are separate and can run alongside each other. The workplace process deals with employment consequences; the criminal route deals with the offence.

bank.question: An HR head setting up the Kenya plant's harassment procedure copies the Indian sister company's procedure word for word, including its committee rules, time limits and external bodies. What is the main weakness?
options: Procedures should not mention time limits at all
Appeals can only ever go to the courts
Rules were copied from another country without checking Kenyan law, which has its own requirements and routes
Nothing important; harassment law is essentially the same in every country that has ratified the ILO conventions on work
bank.explanation: Committee make-up, time limits and external routes differ between countries; Kenya's Employment Act, for example, has its own policy requirement. She needs the current local law and legal advice. Procedures should include time limits.

bank.question: During a three-day distributor conference in Cape Town, a regional manager repeatedly makes sexual remarks to a sales officer at the hotel dinner. He argues it 'wasn't at the workplace'. Which is the best view?
options: Work trips and work-related events and social activities are within scope, so the conduct can be dealt with
Hotels are private premises, so harassment rules cannot apply
Only conduct during the official conference sessions counts, since the dinner was a social event outside working hours
The rules apply only if the company owns the hotel
bank.explanation: ILO Convention 190 covers work-related trips, events and social activities, and many national laws have widened 'workplace' in the same way. A company conference dinner is plainly work-related; venue ownership is irrelevant.

bank.question: A trainee pharmacist's area manager sends her messages most nights: 'Hope you reached home safely, beautiful 🙂', followed by 'Online but not replying?' She replies with short 'ok sir' notes and has begun avoiding evening stock counts. He says he was being caring. What is the best assessment?
options: Not harassment, because the messages are polite, express concern for her safety, and she replied to them each time
Likely harassment: persistent, appearance-focused messages from a senior that are plainly unwelcome
Not harassment, because no explicit sexual request was made
Only harassment if she had blocked him first
bank.explanation: Impact and unwelcomeness matter, not intent. 'Ok sir' replies to a boss are not consent, and avoiding work duties shows the effect. An explicit request or blocking him is not required.

bank.question: A branch manager receives a disclosure on Thursday evening that the cash officer has been groping a teller in the strongroom. The teller is scared to come in on Friday. What is the best combination of actions?
options: Tell the teller to take Friday off unpaid while he thinks about it
Confront the cash officer immediately in front of the branch staff so that everyone knows such behaviour will not be tolerated
Support her, explain workplace and police options, keep the accused away from her, and refer to the committee
Ask the teller to write a detailed statement before he can do anything
bank.explanation: The response should support her, explain workplace and criminal routes, and make her safe without penalising her. A public confrontation compromises the process; unpaid leave punishes her; demanding a statement before acting delays safety.

bank.question: Zara's complaint is under way. Her new shift supervisor rates her 'needs improvement' on teamwork because 'the team is uncomfortable around her since the complaint'. What should HR conclude?
options: The rating is valid because teamwork has genuinely suffered, and ratings must reflect the team's real experience
HR should wait until the inquiry ends before looking at the rating
The rating should stand but be explained to her privately
It penalises her for complaining, so it is likely retaliation and should be reviewed
bank.explanation: Rating someone down because colleagues reacted to her complaint penalises the complaint itself, which is retaliation. The issue is the team's conduct, not hers. Waiting lets harm continue.

bank.question: At an office party, a senior director corners a young intern and is visibly making her uncomfortable. You are a mid-level analyst and don't feel safe confronting him. Which response is best?
options: Delegate: quietly alert a senior colleague or HR, and give the intern a reason to step away
Direct: walk over and loudly tell the director, in front of everyone, that he is harassing the intern
Do nothing, since you don't feel safe confronting him
Document: film the scene on your phone and share it with colleagues
bank.explanation: When Direct isn't safe, Delegate (and Distract) still help. Doing nothing leaves the intern alone, and filming and sharing spreads harm and breaches her privacy.

bank.question: A woman sales officer tells her male peer about repeated comments from a client. He immediately calls the client, threatens to 'sort him out', and emails the whole team about it, without asking her. What went wrong?
options: Nothing; strong and immediate action is exactly what an ally should take, and telling the team makes the standard clear
He should have waited until a second incident
He 'rescued' her instead of asking what she wanted, took the decision away from her and exposed her to the whole team
He should have told the client's family instead
bank.explanation: Real allyship starts with listening and following the affected person's lead. Acting without consent and publicising it can make her situation worse and removes her control.

bank.question: An employee wants to show the harassment committee a series of harassing voice notes in a messaging app. Which approach to evidence is strongest?
options: Delete the chat to avoid seeing it again, then describe the messages from memory
Keep the originals, screenshot sender, dates and times, back up the chat and note who received it
Forward the voice notes to a trusted friend so there is a copy elsewhere, then delete the chat to stop seeing them
Record a video summary describing what the voice notes said
bank.explanation: Original messages with sender details, timestamps and a secure backup give the committee reliable evidence. Deleting originals or relying on memory and summaries weakens the case, and forwarding spreads the content.

bank.question: A manager has interim options while an inquiry into a supervisor's conduct is under way. The complainant wants to keep her current shift and role. Which interim step is most appropriate?
options: Temporarily change the accused supervisor's shift or reporting line so the complainant keeps her role
Move the complainant to another shift so the supervisor can continue as normal
Make no change at all, because the accused is presumed innocent until findings and moving him would prejudge the case
Suspend both until the inquiry ends
bank.explanation: Interim steps should protect the complainant without penalising her, so where possible the accused moves, which is not a finding of guilt. Moving her, making no change while she reports to him, or suspending both all punish the person who spoke up.

bank.question: In a 40-member 'Head Office Staff' chat group, a manager shares a 'joke' about women being bad at maths, tagging the new finance analyst, Lucía. Two people laugh. Which response by a peer best reflects the course?
options: React with a thumbs-up to keep the peace, then message Lucía
Leave the group in protest without saying anything
Forward the joke to HR's inbox and the CEO with a complaint in your own name, without speaking to Lucía
Calmly say in the group it isn't okay, check in privately with Lucía, and offer her a screenshot
bank.explanation: Combining Direct, Delay and Document supports Lucía, signals the group norm and leaves reporting decisions with her. Endorsing the joke or leaving silently changes nothing, and reporting without her input takes away her control.

bank.question: A regional head proudly posts on LinkedIn about 'empowering women' but in meetings regularly talks over two women managers and presents their analysis as his own. What is the most accurate description?
options: Real allyship, because public support matters most
Performative allyship: visible support that does not change what happens to the women at work
Sponsorship, because his posts are promoting the women's work to a wide external audience and raising their profile
Benevolent sexism, because he is protecting them
bank.explanation: Allyship is judged by what changes for others. Interrupting and taking credit undermine the women, whatever he posts publicly. Sponsorship means using influence to advance someone, which he is not doing.

bank.question: A team's weekly review is always at 6:30 pm, minutes are always taken by the only woman, and remote staff rarely speak. Which set of changes best applies inclusive-meeting practice?
options: Keep the 6:30 pm slot, which suits most of the team, but let the woman choose each week whether she takes the minutes
Make the meeting optional for anyone with family duties
Move it into working hours, rotate note-taking, and invite remote participants to speak first on some items
Replace the meeting entirely with email updates
bank.explanation: Scheduling in working hours, sharing chores and actively including remote voices address all three issues. Making it optional for carers excludes them from decisions, and leaving the chore to her keeps the expectation in place.

bank.question: A bank's women's share by level is: trainees 50%, officers 44%, branch managers 18%, area heads 12%, regional heads 10%. The CEO proposes a 'women in leadership' programme for area heads. Based on the data, what is the best advice?
options: Focus first on the officer-to-branch-manager step, where the share drops by 26 points, while keeping senior support
Focus only on regional heads, since the board sees that level
Focus on recruiting more women trainees, since the pipeline starts there and a bigger intake will flow through every level
Keep the area-head programme; the drop from 18% to 12% is the largest leak
bank.explanation: 44% to 18% is a 26-point fall, far larger than 18 to 12 (6 points) or 12 to 10 (2 points). That broken rung starves every later level. Trainee intake is already at 50%.

bank.question: Men's median monthly pay in a pharma company is USD 4,200 and women's median is USD 3,570. What is the median pay gap, and what does a large unadjusted gap with a near-zero adjusted gap most likely indicate?
options: 17.6%; and it shows women are being paid less than men for identical work in the same grades
18%; the calculation should use the mean instead
15%; women are paid less than men in every grade
15%; the gap comes mainly from women being concentrated in lower-paid roles and grades
bank.explanation: (4,200 − 3,570) ÷ 4,200 = 630 ÷ 4,200 = 15%. If the adjusted (like-for-like) gap is near zero, unequal pay for the same work is not the main driver; the gap reflects which jobs women hold. 17.6% divides by the women's figure.

bank.question: From a pool of 60 eligible women, 9 were promoted; from 120 eligible men, 24 were promoted. What is the promotion-rate ratio, and how should it be read?
options: 0.375; women received 9 promotions against men's 24, so they are promoted at well under half the men's rate
1.33; women are promoted more often than men
0.75; women are promoted at three-quarters of the men's rate from the same eligible pool
0.5; women receive half as many promotions in absolute numbers
bank.explanation: Women: 9 ÷ 60 = 15%. Men: 24 ÷ 120 = 20%. Ratio = 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75. Rates matter, not raw counts: 9 versus 24 promotions alone would mislead because the pools differ in size, and 0.375 divides 9 by 24.

bank.question: In a year, 12 women managers left from an average headcount of 48, and 15 men managers left from an average headcount of 150. What do the attrition rates show?
options: Men leave more, since 15 is more than 12
Women's attrition is 25% against men's 10%, so women managers leave at two and a half times the rate
Women's attrition is 12% and men's 15%
Rates cannot be compared fairly because the two headcounts are so different, so only raw numbers of leavers should be used
bank.explanation: Women: 12 ÷ 48 = 25%. Men: 15 ÷ 150 = 10%. 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5. Comparing raw numbers ignores the very different headcounts, which is why rates are used.

bank.question: A telecom's 'women's leadership' initiative consists of confidence workshops for women officers. Two years later the women's share of first-line managers is unchanged. Which next step is most likely to work?
options: Run the confidence workshops more often and extend them to include presentation skills and networking practice
Conclude that women do not want to be managers
Replace the workshops with a Women's Day event
Audit the first-step nomination and promotion process, add structured criteria and assign sponsors
bank.explanation: The course principle is to fix the leak, not the women. If the broken rung is not moving, the selection process and sponsorship gap are the likely causes. More of the same activity, or assumptions about preference, will not change the outcome.

bank.question: A customer-care centre hires Amani, a transgender woman. A supervisor proposes emailing all staff to explain her 'situation' and her previous name, 'so nobody is confused'. What is the best response?
options: Don't send it: her past name and details are private; agree any message with her
Send it, because full transparency about her background now prevents gossip and awkward questions later
Send it, but only to the team leads
Ask Amani to send the email herself
bank.explanation: Privacy is a core principle: past names and personal details are need-to-know, not for staff circulation. Any communication should be agreed with her and focus on expected conduct, not her identity. Asking her to send it shifts the burden onto her.

bank.question: In a quarterly report, HR presents: '18 bias workshops held, 240 managers trained, day-care partner signed.' The board asks, 'So is it working?' What is missing?
options: More detail on the content and quality of each workshop, including participants' feedback scores and attendance rates
Photographs of the events
Outcome measures, such as representation, promotion rates, attrition and pay gaps, against a baseline
The cost of the day-care partnership
bank.explanation: The report lists activities only. Whether it is working depends on outcomes compared with a baseline. Workshop content, photos and costs do not answer the question.

bank.question: A regional office of 22 staff has only two women. HR plans to publish average pay by gender for each office in a staff newsletter. What is the main concern?
options: Averages cannot be calculated reliably for groups of under 30 people, so the figures would be statistically meaningless
Pay data should never be published
With so few women, individuals could be identified; combine or withhold small groups
Newsletters are not an official channel
bank.explanation: Reporting very small groups can reveal individuals' pay. Aggregate them into larger groups or suppress them. Publishing pay-gap data in general is good practice when privacy is protected.

bank.question: Graham wants a single target: '30% women managers within one year.' Current share is 21% with low turnover in management roles. What is the best advice?
options: Accept it; ambitious targets always motivate
Avoid any targets, since they lead to tokenism
Set the 30% target and meet it by appointing women into the next vacancies, setting aside the usual selection criteria
Set a realistic, dated target based on expected vacancies, with linked actions, owners and quarterly tracking
bank.explanation: Targets work when they are realistic and linked to actions, owners and data. With few vacancies, 30% in a year is not achievable without bypassing merit. Abandoning targets loses accountability.

bank.question: After publicising the code and training managers, a company sees complaints rise from 3 to 11 in a year. Average resolution time fell from 70 to 28 days, no retaliation was reported, and the share of staff who say they would feel safe reporting rose. How should this be read?
options: Positively: the evidence suggests greater trust and a working process, though each case's substance still needs review
Negatively: harassment has nearly quadrupled in a single year, which shows the training and publicity have clearly not worked
Neutrally: complaint numbers carry no information
Negatively: training has caused more harassment
bank.explanation: Complaint counts must be read with other indicators. Faster resolution, no retaliation and higher reported safety point to more trust, not more harassment. Cases still need review for patterns.
